item.title: Week 7 Fantasy Football Sleepers: Jaylin Noel, Tyrone Tracy Jr. among underrated options off the waiver wire
item.description: Scott Pianowski goes over sneaky options off the waiver wire for fantasy football in Week 7.
item.content:encoded:
Germie Bernard, Dameon Pierce and Kendre Miller all were useful in Week 6, so it was one of the better sleeper pages of the year. Let’s see if we can keep the ball rolling with a tricky Week 7 slate.

WR Jaylin Noel vs. Giants (22%): I’m shocked the market hasn’t been more interested in Noel, who has been fantasy-relevant three straight weeks and had a 4-107-1 smash against the Jaguars. Obviously the Texans have added other receivers via trade, but Kayshon Boutte hasn’t done much all year and Marvin Harrison Jr. was on a limited snap count last week. Tank Dell’s return also has to be mentioned, but given how little he’s played the last two years, keep expectations small. With C.J. Stroud playing at a high level, let’s leave the light on for Noel.

RB Tyrone Tracy Jr. at Texans (24%): The Houston defense has been much better against the run this year and I don’t blame anyone who wants to avoid the crowded New York backfield at this time. But Tracy did score two touchdowns on his nine opportunities last week, so you have to figure he’ll get a shot. With four teams on bye, Tracy might sneak into the flex discussion this week.

TE Colby Parkinson at Raiders (1%): With Davante Adams and Terrance Ferguson out multiple weeks, the Rams will have to rely on secondary pass catchers for a while. Perhaps Konata Mumpfield and Tyler Higbee will fill those roles, but let’s keep an open mind for Parkinson, who posted a useful 5-31-1 line last week on six targets. The Raiders’ seam coverage has been poor all year.

RB Kendre Miller vs. Steelers (42%): We try not to repeat players in this sheet, but until Miller pushes past 50% rostered, he’s probably worth a mention. Miller had 10 carries and a touchdown two weeks back, and last week it was 22 touches (even if they went for a modest 70 yards). Solving for opportunity is the first job with backfields, so Miller deserves to be taken seriously, even against a strong Pittsburgh front seven in the NFL Paris Game (9:30 a.m. ET start).

RB Mike Washington Jr. vs Rams (32%): Washington is dealing with back and foot soreness, so track his practice week before committing to anything. But we can’t overlook that Washington has been more explosive than Ashton Jeanty this year, and Washington has double-digit touches in two of his last three games.

QB Geno Smith vs. Dolphins (15%): He’s been inconsistent most of the year, with three starts under 10 fantasy points. But Smith was clicking with rookie WR Omar Cooper Jr. last week, Garrett Wilson remains a strong alpha and the Miami pass defense hasn’t stopped much, giving up a 115.0 passer rating.

WR Omar Cooper Jr. vs. Dolphins (43%): Cooper was a hot waiver-wire pickup after his 6-103-1 smash last week, and keep in mind he had a second touchdown wiped out by a curious penalty. Miami’s inexperienced secondary will be tested by Cooper’s speed and ability to get deep.

WR Ja’Kobi Lane vs. Bengals (17%): We’ll mention Lane as a chance to cut the waiver line for next week — his roster tag will spike if he has a breakout game against Cincinnati. Lane was a buzzy player all summer, he had a Week 1 touchdown wiped out by penalty and his return from injury last week was solid (4-40-0, five targets), especially given the presence of backup QB Tyler Huntley. Lane should settle in as Baltimore’s second-best pass catcher in the second half of the year, and Lamar Jackson’s eventual return will pump the upside case.

item.title: Jaguars bye week rooting guide: who should Jacksonville fans cheer for in Week 7?
item.description: Knowing who to cheer for as the Jaguars head into their bye week:
item.content:encoded:
The Jacksonville Jaguars have earned a week off, although their 34-31 loss to the Houston Texans at Wembley Stadium means they probably would have preferred to head into the bye with a little more peace of mind. At 4-2, Jacksonville remains firmly in the AFC South picture, but the Texans have just reminded everyone that this division race is unlikely to be a relaxing experience.

With no Jaguars game to watch this weekend, fans can turn their attention to the rest of the NFL and hope a few results fall Jacksonville’s way. The priorities are straightforward: keep the AFC South rivals in check, avoid giving potential Wild Card competitors unnecessary help, and generally cheer for the NFC when an AFC team is on the other side of the field.

Here is your Week 7 rooting guide, matchup by matchup. You’re welcome, Jaguars fans.

New England Patriots at Chicago Bears (Thursday Night Football)

Root for: Chicago Bears

The Patriots enter Week 7 at 4-2, putting them right in the mix for the AFC East title and a potential Wild Card spot. With Jacksonville holding the same record, there is little reason to help New England improve its position. The Bears are also 4-2, but an NFC victory is the preferable outcome for the Jaguars. Chicago can celebrate all it wants; Jacksonville will happily accept a Patriots loss as a small win of its own.

Pittsburgh Steelers at New Orleans Saints (Paris, France)

Root for: New Orleans Saints

The Steelers are another 4-2 AFC team that Jacksonville could be competing against for playoff positioning later in the season. Pittsburgh has made a solid start, and the last thing the Jaguars need is for it to keep building momentum. New Orleans has had its own struggles, but this is a straightforward rooting interest: give the Saints a reason to celebrate in Paris and send the Steelers home with a loss. If the French crowd can help deliver a little chaos, all the better.

San Francisco 49ers at Atlanta Falcons

Root for: Atlanta Falcons

This one is less about a direct Jacksonville rival and more about taking advantage of an NFC-versus-NFC matchup. San Francisco is unbeaten at 6-0 and looks like one of the NFC’s leading contenders, while Atlanta has had a more difficult start. Neither result directly changes the Jaguars’ AFC standing, so this is a chance to root for the underdog and see whether the Falcons can spoil the 49ers‘ perfect record. Jacksonville fans can enjoy the spectacle without worrying about an AFC rival gaining ground.

Cincinnati Bengals at Baltimore Ravens

Root for: Cincinnati Bengals

This is one of the trickier games of the weekend because both teams are AFC contenders, and somebody has to take the victory. Baltimore is 4-2, while Cincinnati is also firmly in the playoff conversation. A Bengals win would hand the Ravens a damaging loss and potentially tighten the race among the AFC’s Wild Card hopefuls. Neither team is an ideal winner from Jacksonville’s perspective, but if we have to pick one, let’s see Baltimore stumble. The Jaguars have enough to worry about in their own division without the Ravens making life more difficult elsewhere.

Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Carolina Panthers

Root for: Carolina Panthers

This one is a little more complicated than simply backing the NFC team, because there could be a Jacksonville angle worth watching if things continue to unravel in Tampa Bay. The Buccaneers have stumbled to a 1-5 start, putting Todd Bowles under increasing pressure, and if the organization decides to make a change, it could look toward a familiar face from Liam Coen’s coaching tree. Jaguars offensive coordinator Grant Udinski has already emerged as a potential candidate for the job, and Tampa Bay could be tempted to try to poach another of Jacksonville’s rising offensive minds. A Panthers win would pile further pressure on the Buccaneers and potentially make that coaching conversation a little more interesting. Jacksonville fans should be rooting for Carolina here, because the last thing the Jaguars need is an NFC South rival getting ideas about raiding their coaching staff.

New York Giants at Houston Texans

Root for: New York Giants

Here is one of the weekend’s biggest games for Jaguars fans, even if the matchup itself might not immediately jump off the page. Houston just beat Jacksonville at Wembley, cutting into the Jaguars’ advantage in the AFC South. The Texans are 2-4, so the Jags still currently enjoy a lead, but their head-to-head victory makes them a more dangerous opponent than their record suggests. A Giants win would stop Houston from building a winning streak and give Jacksonville a little breathing room while it rests. If the Texans could lose every remaining game without affecting Jacksonville’s own schedule, that would be lovely, too.

Indianapolis Colts at Minnesota Vikings

Root for: Minnesota Vikings

The Colts are another AFC South rival, which makes this one simple. Indianapolis is 2-4 and has already lost ground in the division, but Jacksonville should not give it an opportunity to recover. Minnesota is unbeaten at 5-0 and has been one of the NFL’s strongest teams, so the Vikings are well positioned to take care of business at home. A Colts loss would keep them well behind the Jaguars and make the division race a little less stressful. The departure of Indy’s GM Chris Ballard this week adds a little intrigue, but is largely irrelevant to Jags fans. There is no need to overthink this one: Skol, Vikings.

Miami Dolphins at New York Jets

Root for: Miami Dolphins

Neither AFC East team has made a convincing start, but the Jets have two wins compared with Miami’s winless record. That makes New York the more immediate concern if it can start stringing victories together. A Dolphins win would hand the Jets another loss and help prevent them from becoming a factor in the AFC Wild Card race. Yes, rooting for a winless team might feel strange, but this is a bye week rooting guide, not a popularity contest. If Miami can finally get something going, Jacksonville will gladly take the collateral benefit.

Cleveland Browns at Tennessee Titans

Root for: Cleveland Browns

This is another non-negotiable one. Tennessee is 1-5, but the Titans are still a divisional rival, and Jacksonville needs to keep them down. Cleveland is 4-2 and could be a threat in the AFC Wild Card race, so this is not an entirely comfortable choice. However, the Browns are the better team to back here because a Titans loss is directly beneficial to Jacksonville’s chances of winning the AFC South. The Jaguars cannot afford to take divisional games for granted, even when their rivals are struggling. And let’s be honest – who doesn’t enjoy the misery emanating from Tennessee right now?

Denver Broncos at Arizona Cardinals

Root for: Arizona Cardinals

Denver is 4-2 and another potential competitor for an AFC playoff berth, so Jacksonville would benefit from seeing the Broncos lose. Arizona has struggled in the NFC West, but that is not Jacksonville’s problem. The Cardinals have the opportunity to deliver a useful upset, and the Jaguars will be cheering them on from the sofa. If Arizona can pull it off, Jacksonville gets the result it wants without having to do anything more strenuous than open a bag of snacks. Oh, and Larry Fitz gets his jersey retired too – what’s not to love?

Green Bay Packers at Detroit Lions

Root for: Detroit Lions

This is an NFC North battle, so neither result will directly affect Jacksonville’s position in the AFC. Green Bay is 4-2, while Detroit is also in the hunt in the NFC. We will lean toward the Lions, hoping they can knock the Packers down a peg and make the NFC North race more competitive. There is no need for Jaguars fans to become experts in NFC tiebreakers this weekend; the main objective is to get through the schedule with as many favorable AFC results as possible.

Los Angeles Rams at Las Vegas Raiders

Root for: Los Angeles Rams

The Raiders are 3-3 and could still emerge as a factor in the AFC playoff race, making a loss useful for Jacksonville. The Rams have struggled in the NFC West, but they are the preferred team here simply because they play in the other conference. A Los Angeles win would push Las Vegas further down the AFC standings and help keep another potential Wild Card challenger at bay. This is not a game that will define Jacksonville’s season, but a Raiders loss is certainly better than a Raiders win.

Kansas City Chiefs at Seattle Seahawks (Sunday Night Football)

Root for: Seattle Seahawks

The Chiefs are unbeaten at 5-0 and currently sit among the AFC’s leading contenders. Kansas City is a team Jacksonville could eventually have to navigate in the playoff picture, and there is no particular reason to help it maintain its perfect record. Seattle is 3-3 and would benefit from a win in the NFC, while a Chiefs defeat would be a welcome development for the AFC race. The Seahawks have the opportunity to make a statement on Sunday night, and Jaguars fans should be hoping they do exactly that. KC are beginning to look like the 2018 version rather than recent iterations; a darkening cloud on the horizon for any potential postseason matchup.

Dallas Cowboys at Philadelphia Eagles (Sunday Night Football)

Root for: Dallas Cowboys

We finish the week with an NFC East rivalry, and there is a reasonable case for either side. Philadelphia is 2-4 after losing to Jacksonville in London and then falling to Carolina, while Dallas is also 2-4 following its defeat in Green Bay. The Eagles’ struggles are particularly relevant because Jacksonville already has that head-to-head win on its résumé, and a Philadelphia victory would help strengthen the value of it. Nevertheless, we will lean toward Dallas here, hoping the Cowboys can push Philadelphia further down the NFC East standings. It is not the most consequential game for Jacksonville, but there is something satisfying about ending the weekend watching Nick Sirianni’s outrageous levels of self-confidence take a hit.

item.title: Broncos vs. Cardinals: 3 Things to Watch in Week 7
item.description: The Denver Broncos head on the road to battle the Arizona Cardinals. Here are three storylines I’ll be watching in their Week 7 matchup.
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos battle the Arizona Cardinals for their Week 7 matchup of the 2026 regular season. Both teams are coming off victories due to great play on defense. However, each have a lot to sort out on offense. Here are three storylines I’ll be monitoring closely on Sunday.

The return of edge rusher Jonathon Cooper

The Broncos were the top team in the NFL the past two seasons when it came to sacking opposing quarterbacks. However, there has been a slight dip in production so far this season. Defensive lineman John Franklin-Myers leaving in free agency was one of them. Edge rusher Jonathon Cooper being on the Commisioner’s Exempt List for the first six games of the season is another.

While Cooper and the Broncos likely won’t get finality on his ongoing legal situation until next year, we do know he is poised to make his regular season debut this weekend against the Cardinals. And the timing couldn’t have been any better.

Third-year edge rusher Jonah Elliss, who replaced Cooper as a starter, hobbled off the field in the Broncos’ thrilling overtime victory versus the Seattle Seahawks. Elliss was seen in a boot and crutches at the Utah vs. Colorado collegiate game over the weekend. It’s safe to say he will be missing a few games.

With Cooper back in the fold, that should help bolster their pass rush. His sack productivity did decline toward the end of last season, but he still boasted some of the best hurry and pressure rates amongst edge rushers. I think Denver’s run defense will also be better with him in the mix. I’m looking forward to seeing him play.

What version of Bo Nix will show up on Sunday?

To say that quarterback Bo Nix is experiencing some regression this season may be putting it mildly. A few days ago, Head Coach Sean Payton was asked whether or not he was considering making a switch at the position. Payton stood behind his third-year signal caller and pointed out that there are a bunch of issues on offense that need to be fixed.

“No. He’s going to become the byproduct of all the finer things that get improved. The improved play from our offensive line, the more efficient we are relative to balance, running the football. That’s our jobs as coaches here. We talked after the game about we’re excited to get that win, and yet at the same time find that improvement we need in all areas. So, it starts with all of us,” stated Payton.

Though it’s clear Nix needs to improve drastically moving forward in order for the Broncos to be a contender. I’m trying to remain optimistic. He has struggled early on in his first two seasons, but has got better in the second half stretch. That gives me some hope moving forward.

Perhaps the Cardinals game will provide an opportunity to see the old Bo Nix. The Cardinals had a good defensive performance against the Rams in Week 6, but that unit has not been strong most of the season. They currently rank 22nd in the NFL in pass yards allowed per game. Moreover, are one of the worst in the NFL on stopping opponents on third down.

Will Nix finally start showing some promise and help guide Denver to a win? That’s one thing I’ll be monitoring.

Who steps up to lead the way in the Broncos’ backfield?

As Payton noted, the struggles on offense aren’t all Bo Nix. When you look at Denver’s running game to start their 2026 gridiron campaign compared to where they were at last season through the same stretch—it’s a huge difference. The Broncos touted one of the top rushing attacks in the NFL in the first portion of last season. This year, they are one of the worst.

That isn’t an excuse for Nix’s issues, but everyone knows he would operate a tad better with a better ground game. All quarterbacks do. As I authored earlier today, Denver needs to run the ball with authority. That means the offensive line has to do a much better job with their run blocks. Moreover, the running backs need to perform much better too.

J.K. Dobbins has really struggled. Last season, he averaged five yards per carry. So far this year, he is posting a 3.3 yard per carry average. Second-year running back RJ Harvey has shown some flashes, but the long runs and explosive plays haven’t been there. Rookie running back Jonah Coleman is eligible to come off short-term injured reserve this week. If healthy, he could provide a spark for Denver’s rushing attack and help them grind out another victory.

item.title: 12 trade deadline targets who could help the Seahawks make a run
item.description: From Quenton Nelson to Khalil Mack, 12 trade targets could help Seattle fix its biggest weaknesses.
item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Seahawks don’t need to make a trade just because the deadline is approaching. But after a 3-3 start, an offense that has struggled to find consistency, and two difficult games against the Kansas City Chiefs and Chicago Bears ahead, John Schneider has plenty of reasons to explore the market.

The NFL trade deadline is November 10. By then, Seattle should have a much clearer idea of what this team can realistically accomplish. If the Seahawks lose both upcoming games and fall to 3-5, the front office will have to confront an uncomfortable question: is this roster one or two additions away from getting back on track, or are the problems too widespread for a deadline deal to fix?

The timing of the Indianapolis Colts’ decision to fire general manager Chris Ballard makes that question even more interesting. Ed Dodds, a former Seahawks executive who worked under Schneider, is now overseeing Indianapolis’ personnel department on an interim basis. That doesn’t guarantee a trade between the two teams, but it creates an opportunity worth examining.

Running back: Should Seattle spend big on a star?

The Seahawks’ ground game has been a major concern. Kenneth Walker III departed in free agency, first-round rookie Jadarian Price has been dealing with an injury, and Zach Charbonnet has also been unavailable. Seattle has struggled to replace Walker’s production, leaving the offense without the balance it needs.

Jonathan Taylor is an obvious name to consider. He remains one of the league’s most productive backs, with 1,585 rushing yards and 18 touchdowns in 2025. Through six games in 2026, he has 492 rushing yards and seven touchdowns.

Taylor’s combination of acceleration, vision, contact balance and finishing ability would give Seattle a runner capable of creating yards even when the blocking isn’t perfect. He could transform the backfield and take some pressure off the passing game. There is also a historical connection. Taylor was a popular potential target for Seattle in the 2020 draft, and footage of him expressing interest in the Seahawks has resurfaced amid the trade speculation.

However, Taylor is not an expiring-contract player. He is under contract through 2028, with $16 million owed in 2027. A deal would likely cost at least a second-rounder plus additional compensation. Seattle would be making a substantial financial and draft investment in a position with a short career window.

That is where the argument against a Taylor trade becomes important. The Seahawks already used a first-round pick on Price, and both Price and Charbonnet are expected to return. They also have future extensions to consider, including defensive tackle Byron Murphy II.

Saquon Barkley offers a comparable high-end alternative. His 2024 season was extraordinary, with 2,005 rushing yards in the regular season and a Super Bowl championship with Philadelphia. His production fell to 1,140 rushing yards in 2025, and he has been limited to four games in 2026 by a hamstring injury.

Barkley is a versatile runner and receiver who could give Seattle another explosive weapon. But the injury situation, contract and acquisition price would all need to be evaluated carefully. The Eagles would also have to be willing to move a player who remains a major part of their offense.

Tony Pollard is a more economical possibility. He has surpassed 1,000 rushing yards in four seasons and could offer a dependable veteran presence. He wouldn’t solve the offense’s structural problems, but he could strengthen the rotation and reduce the pressure on inexperienced or returning players.

Omarion Hampton is a different kind of gamble. The Chargers selected him in the first round in 2025, and he has shown potential despite a modest statistical start to his NFL career. A change of scenery could help, but Los Angeles invested too much in him to move on without a meaningful offer.

Edge rusher: Khalil Mack could make the defense even better

The Seahawks’ defense has generally been more reliable than the offense, but the edge rush has not produced consistently enough. Mike Macdonald’s scheme can generate pressure from the interior, yet Seattle still needs players who can win from the outside.

Dante Fowler was a reasonable low-cost gamble, but his impact has been limited. If the Seahawks want to improve their ability to pressure quarterbacks in critical situations, Khalil Mack is an obvious target.

Mack has three sacks and five tackles for loss through six games in 2026. The veteran is playing on a one-year, $18 million contract with the Chargers, who have struggled badly enough to invite questions about whether they might consider moving veterans.

Mack would bring proven pass-rush ability, strength against the run and experience in high-leverage situations. He could also help Seattle manage the workload and maintain a higher level of pressure throughout the game.

The cost would matter. Other contenders would likely be interested in a player with Mack’s résumé. Still, if Los Angeles makes him available, this is the kind of short-term acquisition that could improve Seattle without requiring a long-term commitment.

YaYa Diaby is another possibility. He recorded nine sacks and 62 pressures in 2025, but has started slowly in 2026, with no sacks and seven pressures. Diaby is younger than Mack and offers more long-term upside, particularly because his contract is expiring. He also has the athleticism and run-defense ability to fit Macdonald’s scheme. The uncertainty is whether Tampa Bay would actually sell, and whether Seattle would be willing to pay enough to beat competing offers.

Carl Granderson could provide another option. He recorded six sacks in 2025 and has 2.5 through four games this season. His size and ability to defend the run make him an interesting fit, although his contract runs through 2027, so he would not be a rental. New Orleans also has its own division race to consider.

Will McDonald IV would offer explosive speed, but the New York Jets exercised his fifth-year option, making him a more complicated and potentially expensive target.

Cornerback: The value of insurance

Brandon Stephens is worth monitoring if the Jets become sellers. He spent four seasons in Baltimore, including the period when Macdonald was part of the Ravens’ coaching staff. That familiarity could ease his transition, although it would not automatically make him a perfect fit.

Cam Hart of the Chargers is a more developmental option. His size and physical profile are intriguing, but Seattle would need to determine whether he is ready to contribute consistently.

Kelee Ringo of the Eagles is the speculative alternative. He entered the league with considerable potential after playing at Georgia, but has yet to become a consistent contributor. A change of scenery could help, particularly if the acquisition cost is low.

Quenton Nelson: The opportunity Seattle shouldn’t ignore

If the Seahawks are serious about improving the offense, Quenton Nelson may be the most compelling target available.

Nelson is 30 years old, a six-time first-team All-Pro and an eight-time Pro Bowler. He is in the final year of his current contract, making him a different proposition from Taylor.

Nelson has a elite zone-blocking performance and the possibility of acquiring him for a second-round pick, similar to what Seattle paid for Leonard Williams in 2023. Maybe Anthony Bradford could be included in a package, giving Indianapolis a younger guard to evaluate while Seattle opens a spot for Nelson.

Nelson would also force a decision about Grey Zabel. Both players are left guards, so Seattle would need to consider moving Zabel to right guard or exploring another reshuffle. The important point is that the adjustment is manageable. Seattle should not reject the opportunity to acquire an elite guard simply because it would require changes elsewhere on the line.

The comparison with Leonard Williams is especially strong. Williams arrived in Seattle in his late twenties on an expiring contract, and the Seahawks paid a second- and fifth-round pick to acquire him. The team later re-signed him, and he became a key defensive player.

Nelson could follow a similar path. Seattle would acquire a high-level veteran, give him a chance to experience the organization, and attempt to convince him to stay beyond the season. Even if he eventually left, the team could potentially receive compensatory draft capital.

Final thoughts

Seattle’s recent midseason trade history provides a useful model. Leonard Williams became a defensive cornerstone. Ernest Jones IV helped stabilize the middle of the defense. Rashid Shaheed added a dynamic return threat.

Those deals had different levels of impact, and not every acquisition needs to become a franchise-defining move. The goal is to improve the team without sacrificing too much of its future.

The 3-3 Seahawks are already chasing a 6-0 San Francisco team, and the remaining schedule is another reason to take the next few weeks seriously. The NFC playoff race will also include the Rams and a competitive NFC North.

A 3-5 record after the Chiefs and Bears games would not automatically end Seattle’s season. It would, however, make the case for a major investment harder to defend unless the front office believes a specific player can change the team’s trajectory.

The best approach is to establish a clear priority. Nelson could transform the offensive line. Mack could improve a pass rush that needs more consistency. A running back might give the offense another dimension, while a cornerback could provide insurance against injuries.

One or two smart acquisitions could make a meaningful difference. But the Seahawks should be buying solutions, not headlines. The deadline is an opportunity to improve the roster — not an obligation to spend draft capital.

item.title: Our Offense vs. Their Defense: Pittsburgh Steelers
item.description: An intriguing matchup in Paris as the Saints offense will take on a strong Steelers defense
item.content:encoded:
Bonjour, Who Dat Nation!

The Saints have traveled across the world and will find their offense going up against one of the best defenses in the league. The Steelers’ defense is a top-10 unit overall, and the matchup advantages they have could allow them to exploit the biggest issue with the Saints’ offense.

The Steelers’ defense is led by a legend in the making, T.J. Watt. So far this season, Watt has 4.5 sacks, 6 tackles for loss, and 15 total tackles. He also has a forced fumble and an interception, which he returned for a touchdown. The Steelers’ defensive unit as a whole has 16 sacks on the season, which ranks in the top 10 in the league. They are also in the top 10 in turnover differential at +3 on the season.

The Steelers’ defense is what is carrying the team. So far, no opponent has been able to score more than 27 points against them. They feature elite players at every level, including Watt and Alex Highsmith as pass rushers, along with Jalen Ramsey, who can play all over the secondary.

This is not a matchup that will be easy for the Saints. If anything, the Steelers may very well be able to exploit the Saints’ biggest weakness, which is the offensive line.

The Saints average 224 passing yards per game, while the Steelers allow only 204 passing yards per game. The Steelers average about 2.7 sacks per game, while the Saints are allowing 2.17. Having Asim Richards on the offensive line against T.J. Watt and Alex Highsmith is something Kellen Moore will have to prepare for.

The Steelers’ rushing defense does present an opportunity for the Saints to have some success, as Pittsburgh is allowing 103.2 rushing yards per game. Unfortunately, the Saints are averaging only 97.3 rushing yards per game. The Saints were able to establish a running game last week against the Giants and will have to do so again in Paris. If they are unable to establish the run, it will put them in obvious third-and-long situations.

If the Saints are going to win this game, they will have to make sure to utilize motion to identify coverages, establish the running game early, and keep the offense on schedule. Third-and-long situations are a recipe for disaster against a pass rush this dangerous, especially with an offensive line that has obvious protection issues.

There is some excitement building around the possibility that Jordyn Tyson could make his season debut this week since he traveled with the team. If he is able to play in this game, it would be a big addition, giving the Saints another weapon in the passing game. Tyson is also a very willing blocker at the receiver position and could help improve the running game a little bit as well, especially if the Saints are able to get their running backs to the edge.

This will be a big test for the Saints’ offense and coaching staff. Hopefully, they are fully prepared and up for the task.

How do you think the Saints’ offense matches up against the Steelers’ defense? Share your thoughts in the comments.

item.title: Will the Giants unmask C.J. Stroud?
item.description: During the offseason, there was no lack of hate, vitriol and utter ignorance thrown at Houston Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud. After the team’s unceremonious exit from the 2025 NFL playoffs, many fans, talking heads and know-it-alls blamed Stroud for everything from losing the game against the New England Patriots to dooming the franchise for all […]
item.content:encoded:
During the offseason, there was no lack of hate, vitriol and utter ignorance thrown at Houston Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud. After the team’s unceremonious exit from the 2025 NFL playoffs, many fans, talking heads and know-it-alls blamed Stroud for everything from losing the game against the New England Patriots to dooming the franchise for all eternity.

As the old adage goes, the quarterback gets too much praise and too much shade.

There’s no real point in rehashing all the data-points that Stroud was far from the only reason Houston didn’t advance to the AFC Championship last year.

However, it is fun to look at his current 2026 season and say a hearty “told you so” to all the haters who said he sucks. Ha!

NFL Communications

OFFENSE: QB C.J. STROUD, HOUSTON TEXANS

Stroud completed 24 of 34 pass attempts (70.6 percent) for 312 yards and three touchdowns for a 116.3 passer rating in Houston’s 34-31 win against Jacksonville at Wembley Stadium. He was the only quarterback with a passer rating of 115-or-higher in Week 6. Stroud is one of four quarterbacks this season with at least 300 passing yards, three touchdown passes, a completion percentage of 70-or-higher and a passer rating of 110-or-higher in a single game.

This is Stroud’s fourth Offensive Player of the Week award. He becomes the third Texans player to earn the honor at least four times, joining Deshaun Watson (five-time winner) and Matt Schaub (four).

Stroud joins Eddie George as the only former Ohio State players to win Offensive Player of the Week four times.

C.J. Stroud’s stats are definitely elite so far in 2026. Not only has Stroud overcome the naysayers, he’s won over the wider world of NFL talking heads and casual fans, forcing himself into the MVP conversation this season.

Watching his highs and lows, we see:

better pre-snap reads

better adjustments

an elevated understanding of what the defense is doing

some really slick mis-direction (via pump fakes, head shakes and body aiming)

improved release time.

And best of all, his response to adversity has taken an upswing, possibly due to Andre Johnson’s criticism of how he handled it in the past.

Heading into this weekend’s matchup with the seemingly revitalized New York Giants, history is not in Stroud’s favor.

The Texans are 1-5 vs the G-Men all time, having lost the last 5 straight. However, they’ve not seen the NFC East team since November of 2022, a season we’d all love to forget.

Giants QB J.J. McCarthy, drafted as the savior of the Minnesota Vikings, put on a passing clinic last weekend. If Demeco Ryans can’t get this defense to stop operating like a wet paper bag, McCarthy might have another career game this weekend.

However, the current Texans offense is a far cry from the 2022 version. And Stroud will have Nico Collins, Jalin Noel, Marvin Harrison Jr., Kayshon Boutte and TANK DELL to play catch with this weekend.

That’s right, after nearly 2 years, lightning bolt in cleats receiver Tank Dell returns to the field this weekend.

And, as much as I’ve not been enamored with Texans offensive coordinator Nick Caley, he is growing as both a coach and a play caller. If he’s thinking what a lot of people are thinking, Dell’s first game back will see the speedster blow the top off the defense, create distractions and open up opportunities for Collins, Harrison Jr. and the rest of the receivers.

The Giants have a stingier passing defense (190 yards per game) than their rushing D (135.5 ypg) so far, but they haven’t seen Stroud and his healthy receiving targets yet. And, these stats are likely due to a less than robust passing attack from Big Blue until McCarthy caught fire last week.

A home game, with Stroud on a roll, a “Greatest Show on Turf – Texas Edition” passing attack and a stadium decked out in Battle Red? This has all the makings of another 300+ air yards affair for the good guys.

To the opening question: Will the Giants unmask C.J. Stroud? the answer is a resounding no.

Prediction: New York Giants vs Houston Texans

At the end of the day, J.J. McCarthy is a long way from becoming C.J. Stroud. Unfortunately, the Texans defense has regressed to the mean, meaning McCarthy will still have plenty of big play opportunities. In the end, the wide receiving corps of Houston keeps their QB in the MVP talks.

New York Giants – 31

Houston Texans – 42

item.title: Panthers vs Buccaneers: Storylines to watch
item.description: Breaking down all the big storylines in this week’s matchup!
item.content:encoded:
The Carolina Panthers currently lead the NFC South, and while every storyteller in the media is talking about them being kings of the division, there are still many important games to play, and this is one of them. While the Bucs have felt the bite of injuries, they are currently only two and games back from being tied for the lead in wins. All it takes is for one slate of games to go their way for them to be competing deep into the end of the season. The Panthers are playing good football, and they have to keep it going. Let’s dive right into the storylines for this week’s game.

Offense: Bryce Young needs to keep up the passing party

The Panthers have one of the best passing offenses from basically every yardage category. And while Chuba Hubbard has also been extremely productive leading the rushing attack all season, he’ll be facing one of the better rushing defenses in football. Per Teamrankings.com , their rushing defense ranks as 2nd in yards per rush, 3 in rushes per game, 2 in rush yards per game, and 2 in rushing TDs per game. While you might think this is a result of simply being a bad football team this year, every loss they’ve had ended up being one score games. Teams tend to run the football more when games are close, but they’ve been very productive. I would expect the Panthers to have a bit more trouble running the football this week, even if they are playing their second straight backup quarterback on the other side of the ball. Their passing defense is much more susceptible, so Bryce Young and OC Brad Idzik should resume the aggressiveness in the air, but if the rushing attack isn’t playing the complimentary football that Dave Canales always preaches about, their could be a lot more pressure for Bryce to continue this unreal campaign.

Defense: Pass rush will need to get creative again

Dave Canales announced this week that EDGE Jaelan Phillips is set to miss this week. That leaves an already banged up group of edge rushers down their best man. And while Phillips is obviously a big part of getting pressure on the quarterback as a rusher, he’s equally more important in collapsing the pocket and setting up other pass rushers with good matchups they can win. I’ve been very impressed with 2025 rookie Princely Umanmielen, but what made the biggest difference in this past game in Philadelphia was an extremely aggressive blitzing game plan by DC Ejiro Evero. And he’ll likely have to do that again, dialing up guys like Devin Lloyd an Bobby Okereke from the linebacking spots and sending their multi-talented group of safeties on blitzes.

Bonus storyline: Get a grip on the darn penalties!

The Panthers were called for a franchise record 149 yards of penalties against the Eagles, which luckily didn’t cause them to lose the game. Penalties have been a massive issue with this team all season, and they can’t get away with this and not have it come back to bite them. Whether they are playing Jalon Daniels or a beat up Baker Mayfield this week, it could and should be a very close game based on how the Bucs schedule has gone. A poorly timed penalty could very much tip the scales out of their favor in what could be an ugly contest.

What are you watching for this week, Panthers fans?

item.title: AFC North Week 5 recap: Browns knock Ravens off their perch
item.description: The Browns took the lead in the AFC North by beating the Ravens.
item.content:encoded:
The Ravens lost their spot at the top of the division after falling to the Browns in Week 5, while the Steelers pulled off a comeback win, and the Bengals enjoyed a bye week.

Cleveland Browns (4-2)

Cleveland now sits atop the AFC North after defeating Baltimore, 13-10.

The Browns’ offense struggled to get anything going for most of the game. Cleveland’s lone touchdown of the day came from Austin Estime after a fourth-quarter fumble recovery set the offense up at the 35-yard line. Deshaun Watson struggled heavily against the Ravens’ defense, going 16 of 26 for 164 yards while being sacked five times. Jerry Jeudy was the most productive of the Browns’ wide receivers, catching four passes for 69 yards, including a 33-yard reception to get the offense in range for the game-winning field goal. Jaleel McLaughlin led a banged-up backfield with nine carries and 41 of the team’s 93 rushing yards.

Cleveland’s defense rebounded in a big way after allowing 10 points on Baltimore’s first two drives. The Ravens’ offense, led by backup quarterback Tyler Huntley, struggled to move the ball for the remainder of the game while Derrick Henry was effectively neutralized on the ground, even without Browns star defensive tackle Mason Graham in the lineup. Reigning Defensive Rookie of the Year Carson Schwesinger, who was questionable with an ankle injury, led his team with 13 total tackles and forced the critical fumble on Henry in the fourth quarter. Quincy Williams, Isaiah McGuire, and Maliek Collins accounted for the Browns’ three sacks on Huntley. Andre Szmyt missed his first field goal of the season while making two others, including the game-winner on the final drive of the game.

Pittsburgh Steelers (4-2)

Pittsburgh rallied from a 13-0 deficit to beat the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in overtime, 26-19.

The Steelers scored just three points in the first half before ripping off 23 in the final two quarters and overtime. Aaron Rodgers’s two passing touchdowns brought him to 539 in his career, tying Peyton Manning for the third-most in NFL history. The 42-year-old completed 33 of his 49 passing attempts on the game for 253 yards and an interception to go along with his pair of scores. Jaylen Warren led the ground attack with 50 yards on 14 rushes, while a returning Rico Dowdle chipped in 40 yards on seven carries. D.K. Metcalf led all receivers with 93 yards on 11 catches, trailed closely by rookie Germie Bernard’s 87 yards and a touchdown on 11 receptions. Tight end Darnell Washington also had a touchdown catch to go with 25 yards on four catches.

The Steelers’ defense feasted against backup quarterback Jalon Daniels. Jalen Ramsey and Nick Herbig each had two sacks and Yahya Black had one, while Jamel Dean and Daylen Everette each came away with an interception. Payton led the defense with 11 tackles, bringing him up to 55 on the season, the eighth-most in the league. Chris Boswell finished 4 for 5 on field goals, bringing his number of missed kicks up to four for the season and putting him on pace for a career-high.

Baltimore Ravens (4-2)

Baltimore lost the division lead with a 13-10 loss in Cleveland.

Lamar Jackson’s second straight absence from the offense was glaring as Huntley struggled for much of the day, finishing 19 of 31 for 165 yards and a touchdown. Zay Flowers was the leading receiver with 66 yards on six catches, while rookie Josh Cuevas caught Baltimore’s only touchdown. Derrick Henry failed to get going on the ground after a strong start, rushing 17 times for just 58 yards with a costly fumble that led to Cleveland’s only touchdown. Rookie Ja’Kobi Lane impressed in his return to action after suffering a wrist injury in the season opener, converting first downs on all four of his catches for a total of 40 yards.

Baltimore’s defense was suffocating for much of the game. The pass rush was effective against Deshaun Watson, sacking him five times. Trey Hendrickson logged his second sack as a Raven after a two-game absence due to finger surgery; Nnamdi Madubike, Roquan Smith, Tavius Robinson, and Calais Campbell all got to Watson as well. As usual, though, cracks began to form where they always do: on third down, in the fourth quarter. Jerry Jeudy’s 33-yard catch moved Cleveland into field goal range for Andre Szmyt’s game-winner. That also set up a contrast with Ravens kicker Tyler Loop, who renewing discussions about his job security by missing his third field goal of the season in a game decided by three points.

Cincinnati Bengals (3-2)

The Bengals rested up during their early bye week and will look to join the AFC North’s four-win club on Sunday in Baltimore.

item.title: Bengals Progress Report: Grading the Defense
item.description: A grade for the defense after the first five weeks of the season.
item.content:encoded:
The first five weeks of the 2026 NFL season are in the books, and the Cincinnati Bengals are coming out of their bye week with a 3-2 record. They’re absolutely still “in it,” but they’ve been a mixed bag so far.

After missing the playoffs for the third consecutive season in 2025, the Bengals completely rebuilt their defense. They traded the No. 10 overall pick to the New York Giants for Dexter Lawrence and signed Boye Mafe, Jonathan Allen, Bryan Cook, and Kyle Dugger in free agency.

Unfortunately, after starting 2-0 and looking like everything was heading in the right direction, the Bengals spent the next two weeks repeatedly shooting themselves in the foot.

Then, against the 0-4 Dolphins, they squeaked out an ugly win in which the defense surrendered 24 points to arguably the worst team in football. Before facing Cincinnati, the most points Miami had scored in a game was 13.

So, yeah. Mixed bag.

Here’s a progress report for the defense, starting with the…

RUN DEFENSE

The Bengals started the season doing an excellent job limiting explosive plays on the ground. The longest run they allowed to a running back against the Buccaneers and Texans was just 13 yards.

That changed in Week 3 against the Steelers.

Over the next three games, the Bengals surrendered runs of 35, 25, 39, 26 and 22 yards. Suddenly, a defense that had been effective at preventing big plays was giving them up with alarming regularity.

Lawrence has been outstanding against the run. Even when he isn’t directly involved in a tackle, he’s often occupying two blockers, which should create opportunities for his teammates to make plays.

Unfortunately, someone doesn’t always get the job done.

Missed tackles have once again become a significant problem for Cincinnati’s defense. According to PFF, the Bengals have a tackling grade of just 50.3, the seventh-worst mark in the NFL, and have been credited with 47 missed tackles.

That’s simply not good enough.

With the Bengals returning from their bye week, they’ll play their second divisional game of the season, this time against Derrick Henry, Lamar Jackson, and the Baltimore Ravens.

AFC North games are typically messy affairs, but Cincinnati absolutely cannot allow Henry and Jackson to get going on the ground. If they do, the Bengals risk spending much of the afternoon watching helplessly as Burrow and the offense remain stuck on the sidelines.

Run-Defense Grade: 75% (C)

PASS DEFENSE

Pass defense really consists of two components: the ability to cover receivers and the ability to rush the passer.

The Bengals have been very good at one of those things.

The other? Not so much.

Cincinnati’s defense has brought opposing quarterbacks down in the backfield 17 times through five games, tied for the third-most sacks in the NFL. That puts them on pace for approximately 58 sacks over a full regular season.

For perspective, that’s 16 more sacks than the Bengals recorded during the 2021 regular season, when they eventually reached Super Bowl LVI.

So, clearly, that part of the defense is working.

Unfortunately, when the pass rush doesn’t get home, the defensive backs left on islands have struggled to keep opposing receivers from getting open.

Take the Steelers game, for example.

Aaron Rodgers, who is 42 years old, was somehow able to scramble around the backfield and evade pressure like he was Burrow’s age. When he extended plays, Cincinnati’s secondary struggled to maintain coverage, allowing Pittsburgh to move the ball effectively through the air.

Of course, the Bengals couldn’t stop the run in that game, either, so there was plenty of blame to go around.

Evaluating pass defense can be tricky because there are so many moving parts. A great pass rush can make an average secondary look outstanding, while poor coverage can make even an effective pass rush look inadequate.

With that in mind, I’m breaking the pass defense into two separate grades.

Pass-Rush Grade: 94% (A)
Pass-Coverage Grade: 78% (C+)
Overall Pass-Defense Grade: 86% (B)

There’s a reasonable argument that the Bengals missed the playoffs in 2023 primarily because of Burrow’s injury.

The same excuse can’t be made for 2024 or 2025.

Following the 2024 season, the front office fired defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo, hoping a change in leadership would fix the defense’s problems. Unfortunately, those issues persisted in 2025 under his replacement, Al Golden.

Rather than make another change, the Bengals decided to trust the process, retain Golden and give him considerably more talent to work with. So far, the results have been mixed.

Of course, injuries haven’t helped matters. Bryan Cook, Jordan Battle, and Kyle Dugger have all dealt with injuries, while Jalen Davis and Ja’Sir Taylor are on injured reserve.

Still, injuries or not, the defense hasn’t consistently performed at the level expected of a unit that received such a significant offseason investment.

Fortunately, the Bengals got an early bye week to get healthy, evaluate what’s working, and iron out some of the issues that have plagued them through the first five games. And they’d better take advantage of it. Taylor and his entire coaching staff have a lot riding on this season. It would be difficult to imagine the Bengals allowing four of the prime years of Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase, and Tee Higgins to slip away without a single playoff appearance and still deciding Taylor is the right man for the job.

The offense has the firepower to compete with anyone in the league, but that won’t matter if the defense continues to give away explosive plays and miss tackles.

Taylor needs this defense to get right coming out of the bye.

Otherwise, he could find himself in serious trouble when the regular season comes to an end.

Overall Defensive Grade: 81% (B-)

So, how would you grade the defense? Sound off in the comments section!

item.title: Los Angeles Chargers news: Omarion Hampton still ranked highly among 2nd-year backs

It’s been a rough season thus far for Omarion Hampton.

NFL insider Jordan Schultz at one point made a bold prediction that Hampton would lead the NFL in scrimmage yards while finishing with 12+ touchdowns. “Omarion Hampton has had little opportunity to establish a rhythm.”

“When the 23-year-old was drafted 22nd overall last year, it was with the expectation that he would be the Chargers’ lead back from the jump. He was widely considered a first-round talent after a wildly productive two-season stretch at North Carolina.”

“An ankle injury sidelined Hampton for almost half his rookie season, but he was effective when available. He averaged 4.4 yards per carry, scored five touchdowns and contributed just under 82 total yards per game.Then 2026 rolled around, and the wheels came off.”

“The winless Chargers are a mess, and Mike McDaniel’s decision to use a three-back committee has done little to help Hampton find his groove.Hampton has exceeded 15 carries just once this season, while his yards-per-carry average has dropped by nearly a full yard.”

item.title: NFL cancels Steelers Fan House event in Paris
item.description: The NFL's approach to Sunday's game in Paris has been to shrug and say, "fi des torpilles."
item.content:encoded:
The NFL's approach to Sunday's game in Paris has been to shrug and say, "fi des torpilles."

Meanwhile, the ongoing unrest has resulted in the cancellation of a Steelers Fan House planned for the days preceding the game.

Via Andrew Fillippoini of 93.7 The Fan in Pittsburgh, the NFL has canceled the event.

"Following recent events in the Bastille neighborhood, and after careful consideration, we felt it appropriate not to move forwardwith the planned Steelers Fan House event in Paris," the notice posted by Fillipponi explains.

The message reiterates that preparations for the Steelers-Saints game "continue as planned, with the NFL working closely with local authorities and partners on all operational and security matters."

It's fair to ask why the NFL is being so insistent about proceeding with the Paris game in light of the ongoing issues. However small the chance of a problem may be, it's more than zero percent. While the teams will surely have full security at their hotels and at the stadium and during the trips between the two locations, the fans won't be fully secure until they enter the perimeter at the venue.

Meanwhile, any efforts to enhance security at the stadium will necessarily result in fewer resources available to the rest of the city.

While different from the Jalen Hurts situation, there's a common thread. There's a "show must go on" stubbornness that invites unnecessary risk. But with an inflexible top-down directive to proceed, the NFL is proceeding.

Even if the better approach would be to shift the game to London and go back to Paris next year, or whenever it's possible to play the game when the risk of any potential situations is as close to zero as possible.

item.title: 5 questions with a Bears expert: How is Caleb Williams looking?
item.description: We spoke with SB Nation’s Bears blog about the upcoming Patriots opponent.
item.content:encoded:
Led by second-year head coaches and first-round quarterbacks drafted in 2024, and owning identical 4-2 records, the New England Patriots and Chicago Bears are quite similar to one another. On Thursday night, they will share the field for a prime time matchup — the second between the two clubs in the last three years.

To find out more about the Patriots’ opponent, we spoke with Bill Zimmerman of Pats Pulpit’s sister site Windy City Gridiron, the SB Nation community for all things Bears.

1. I know it’s a small sample size, but how has Caleb Williams looked in his second season under Ben Johnson? What changed in his return to the field from when Tyler Bagent was under center?

Without trying to sound too much like a raging homer, Caleb has looked fantastic in year two. If you don’t consider the week two loss to the Vikings, where Caleb got hurt due to significantly wet and sloppy conditions (it didn’t just rain; it was a monsoon), the offense has looked like arguably the best in the league. Mind you, that’s only two games, so it’s not enough to go on, but it’s been that good in the small sample size.

With Case Keenum and Tyson Bagent, the Bears averaged 19 points per game. With Caleb Williams, they’ve averaged 45 PPG in his two full games. Williams is getting to the point where he can stay in the pocket, operate the Ben Johnson system quickly and efficiently, and keep the chains moving. But Caleb also has the ability to break out of the system and ad-lib on his own, where he gets really dangerous and makes many of the huge off-script plays that make all the highlight reels.

Bagent doesn’t have the ability to operate off-script, and he also doesn’t have a strong arm. Bagent needs to operate quickly, and if he doesn’t get the ball out on time, he can’t make up for it either with his arm and ability to operate if the play breaks down. Caleb is the exact opposite. He can be late on a read but make up for it with insane release and arm strength.

With Caleb back and (mostly) healthy, it’s a dangerous two-headed weapon. First, it’s Ben Johnson’s offense and play calling, which everyone in the league knows is elite. But if the play Johnson calls doesn’t have it, the defense still has to deal with what Caleb Williams can do when the play breaks down.

The Bears offense has a chance to really hit some great heights this year with the synergy that Ben and Caleb are developing.

2. How will not having Kyle Monangai affect the Bears’ offense? Who would be the next men up?

Monangai missing is definitely a knock to the offense. He and D’Andre Swift make a great combination, and they complement each other well.

Roschon Johnson would be the guy to fill in. Johnson doesn’t have the speed or shiftiness of Monangai. There are fans I know that call him SlowJo instead of RoJo. He had just 6 yards on five attempts against Green Bay, and last week he was much better with 51 yards on 13 carries, but that still keeps him below the 4.0 threshold. Johnson is a nice blocker, has pretty good hands, and is a good special teamer. But he’s not a guy you want having 10-plus touches in a game.

3. The Bears have been one of the league’s worst deep pass defenses, but their corners seem to be getting healthy. What’s behind those struggles and how much would having all three starters affect Chicago’s ability to defend deep?

What’s behind the Bears’ lack of success from their secondary? I mean, should I say lack of talent? With Kyler Gordon out, the Bears were mostly running out Jaylon Johnson, Tyrique Stevenson, and rookie Malik Muhammad. With Gordon back last week, they have moved Muhammad to play more outside and made them less reliant on the other two.

Reports were really good over the summer that Johnson had recovered from the injuries that plagued him in 2025, and he was back to his old form. That really hasn’t been the case. He’s made occasional plays but has largely looked like a player that may have lost some athleticism and isn’t able to keep up with faster receivers stretching the field.

Stevenson can make plays as well because he’s a pretty aggressive corner. However, Stevenson, between being overly aggressive and lapses in concentration, consistently gets burned on deep balls as well. Having Gordon back gives them a great blitzing weapon and great play at the line of scrimmage, and his presence will limit how much someone like Stevenson has to be on the field. That will help in some regards, but the Bears are going to be susceptible to the deep ball against Drake Maye for sure.

4. What’s makes the Bears such an effective blitzing defense? Has anyone managed to slow them down?

The key to the Bears blitzing is the success they are having with it on third down. The Bears have 17 sacks on the season; nine of them have come on third down. That makes them arguably the best third-down defense in the NFL. Heading into this game, opponents have converted just 26% of their third downs against the Bears, trailing only the Minnesota Vikings.

Defensive Coordinator Dennis Allen has been a wizard with this team on third downs, and that’s not just last year; they were good on third downs last year as well, despite being one of the worst overall defenses in the league.

What’s wild about those nine third-down sacks I mentioned earlier, four have come from defensive backs. You can expect Kyler Gordon to blitz frequently, and with the banged-up Patriots offensive line, it wouldn’t shock me if he gets home for another sack on Thursday night.

Even in the Bears’ losses, the third-down conversion rates sit at 7-for-25, so still close to their averages. It sounds dumb, but the best way to beat the Bears’ third-down success? Stay out of third and long. The Bears can be had on first and second down, so gain yards there, avoid third downs all together or at least keep it to third and short where it’s a quick-hitting play and the blitz doesn’t have a chance to get home.

5. Who do you think pulls out a victory on Thursday night, and why?

I do think the Bears are going to win this one. I think they are carrying a lot of momentum and confidence with Caleb Williams back. I think the offense is clicking, and I do think the Patriots’ defense can cause some issues for them, but I do think they can score on them. I expect Drake Maye to beat the Bears with a few pretty deep balls, but I do think they will make some plays on third down and stop enough Patriots drives.

Thursday games are tricky because they always seem like anything can happen with a short week of preparation. These are two good football teams, so we should expect a close game.

Bears 27, Patriots 24.

item.title: Eagles Film Analysis: Can empty formations help solve the offense’s pressure problems?
item.description: Here’s one suggestion to fix things.
item.content:encoded:
All statistics come from the Fantasy Points Data Suite or from NFL Pro in this one.

A bonus article! The Eagles’ protection sucks right now. Four-weak pressures and other pressure packages are a major part of today’s NFL, and the Eagles desperately need better answers. They cannot keep allowing pressure to destroy the entire operation before the quarterback has a chance to do anything. Whether it’s Jalen Hurts or Tanner McKee, give the quarterback and the players around him a chance to execute.

I’ve posted a full video on Patreon breaking down these issues, combining the numbers with film examples to explain what’s going wrong and what the Eagles could do about it. I’d appreciate you checking it out if you want to learn more about how I use stats and film together, or simply join me in getting increasingly annoyed at how incompetent this offense looks right now. Here’s a little spoiler…

This post shows how straightforward basic self-scouting can be. You don’t need to uncover some revolutionary concept. Look at what happens under pressure, identify where you’ve succeeded, and watch the film to understand why. Then work out whether those successful ideas can become a bigger part of the offense. The numbers should prompt questions, and the film should help answer them.

One obvious place to start is formation. Spread the defense out, make the potential threats easier to identify and give the quarterback clear answers to establish some rhythm. Empty won’t magically fix every protection issue, but there is enough encouraging evidence here to warrant using it more. This stuff shouldn’t be this hard. I’m bored of hearing about the Eagles’ pass protection woes, so I thought I’d look at how formation can help them for the rest of the year.

This isn’t a normal film breakdown for me, but I wanted to look at some statistics and what is going on. As often, this post was inspired by this graph from the wonderful Deniz Selman.

That is one of the most insane graphs I’ve ever seen after 6 weeks of a season. It’s not Week 2 anymore! Anyway, let’s look at some results and what the Eagles can do differently.

What the data shows

Let’s start with the Eagles’ overall results under pressure. Empty has been their most productive formation, while under center (singleback) has been a complete disaster. There are only 12 pressured plays from empty, so nobody should pretend this proves it will solve everything. However, when your offense keeps falling apart under pressure, surely you should explore the situations where it has actually functioned?

Next, look at the target depth under pressure. The intermediate production stands out. Beating pressure doesn’t have to mean throwing behind the line of scrimmage or launching a desperate deep shot. Opportunities exist to attack the space behind the rush, but route combinations, timing, and protection rules must give the quarterback access to those throws. “Get the ball out” means very little without somewhere useful to throw it. There is no surprise that throwing deep or behind the LOS hasn’t worked. The stats match the eye test.

Now let’s narrow it to five-plus rushers generating pressure within 2.5 seconds. Empty still stands out. It’s only four plays, but these are precisely the situations that have been destroying this offense. When pressure arrives that quickly, the answer needs to be built into the play. You cannot expect either quarterback to repeatedly escape and rescue a concept that hasn’t had time to develop. Surely, the staff is looking at this?

Here’s empty against five-plus rushers overall. Spreading the defense out can help the quarterback assess the coverage and potential rush before the snap. It also gives him five receiving options, with opportunities to replace blitzing defenders. That still requires coherent protection and hot routes, particularly when six come against five blockers, but at least it gives the quarterback a lot of information pre-snap. It’s easier when you know only six can blitz. No one is blitzing empty with 7 defenders, so you only have to work out who the +1 rusher can be.

The wider shotgun sample shows that simply putting the quarterback in the gun isn’t enough. Spacing, route distribution, and the number of available receivers matter too. I want an offense that helps McKee to identify the problem and deliver the ball with confidence. Empty is one way to simplify that picture and establish some rhythm.

Then there’s under-center against five-plus rushers. Come on. Fifteen plays without a single successful one is horrendous. Turning your back to the defense on play-action makes it harder to identify and respond to pressure, especially when the protection keeps breaking down. How long do you keep asking players to execute something that produces absolutely nothing?

Finally, this gets even more interesting when you look at the number of route runners against five-plus rushers. With three or fewer, the Eagles average 0.6 yards per play. With four, that rises to 3.5. With five, it jumps to 6.3, alongside positive EPA. These are different play samples, so context matters, but keeping extra players in protection clearly hasn’t guaranteed better results. Sending five out gives the defense more receiving threats to account for and the quarterback more answers. That deserves serious attention. The Eagles’ tight ends and running backs are not good in pass protection. How about we stop asking them to do it?

Final Thoughts

Empty won’t magically fix the Eagles’ protection, but the numbers give them an obvious place to start. Spread things out, build in clear answers, and give McKee and the rest of the offense a chance to find some rhythm. The stats do not lie. The frustrating part is how straightforward this is to identify through basic self-scouting.

If you watch the video on Patreon, all of this takes less than 20 minutes to work out. It’s not difficult. The coaching staff has far more information than we do, yet the same problems keep destroying the offense. At some point, they have to adapt to what is actually happening on the field. Obviously, better players will help improve pass protection, but the Eagles’ coaches have to consider their formation to prevent problems from occurring.

Thank you for reading! I’d love to hear your thoughts, so feel free to comment below and ask any questions.If you would like to support me further, please check out my Patreon here!

item.title: 3 Titans players who could help replace DT Jordan Elliott
item.description: The Tennessee Titans released DT Jordan Elliott after a disturbing situation; we have 3 players who could replace him.
item.content:encoded:
The Tennessee Titans released veteran defensive tackle Jordan Elliott earlier this week. The complete details are now available. A to Z Sports and Easton Freeze reported Elliott allegedly threatened a teammate (reportedly JC Latham) with gun violence, even showing intent before the situation was calmed. Unacceptable stuff. Naturally, the Titans released Elliott even though head coach Robert Saleh vouched for him to receive a future opportunity elsewhere during Wednesday’s presser.

Elliott was playing quality football as a rotational defensive lineman after signing a two-year contract with the team in free agency. Saleh, Aaron Whitecotton, and Mike Borgonzi must deal with the fallout. We’ve identified three Titans players who could help the defensive line replace Elliott.

Nazir Stackhouse

Nose tackle Nazir Stackhouse helped replace Elliott in Sunday’s Week 6 win over the Colts. He served as the primary interior run stopper behind Jeffery Simmons and John Franklin-Myers. Remember, that is essentially the role Elliott was playing. The Titans claimed Stackhouse off waivers from the Green Bay Packers after final cuts. He played well as a big-bodied space eater.

Solomon Thomas

The Titans brought Elliott to Tennessee as a free agent this past offseason partially because he played for Coach Saleh before. Understanding his system is vital to the success of the scheme. Well, following Elliott’s departure, the only Titans interior defender on the roster who has played for Saleh before is veteran DT Solomon Thomas.

Timmy Horne

When the Titans ruled out Elliott for Sunday’s game versus the Colts, they made Timmy Horne a gameday call-up. The four-year pro ended up playing a sizable 25 snaps. Horne is listed as being 312 pounds via the team’s official website; he’s a more traditional nose tackle who can play a similar role to Elliott. With the Titans having an open spot on the 53-man roster following Elliott’s release, promoting Horne from the practice squad would make sense.

item.title: Kyle Shanahan’s former star WR believes he’ll never win a Super Bowl
item.description: The Niners head coach was criticized for one part of his playcalling.
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers are at the top of the NFL right now, sitting at 6-0 after their 23-17 win over the Washington Commanders.

After starting the year with the third-best odds in their own division, the 49ers are the clear frontrunners to win the NFC and currently stand as the favorites to win the Super Bowl at +600, according to FanDuel.

San Francisco has been clicking everywhere this season, despite their bevy of injuries. Behind MVP-level play from Brock Purdy and an elite No. 1 receiver in Mike Evans, the 49ers offense has been quite efficient throughout the year. The defense, on the other hand, has overcome the loss of Nick Bosa over the last few weeks to be a strong finishing team with a ton of growing young talent under Raheem Morris.

Even with the injuries, it feels like this could be the year for the 49ers, and they’ll get a chance to get a lot of players healthy following their bye in Week 8.

Ultimately, it will come down to the playoffs, where the 49ers have had their moments over the last seven years, but have come up short in their pursuit of the Super Bowl. They made it there in 2019, lost in the NFC Championship Game in 2021 and 2022, made it there again in 2023, and then lost in the divisional round last year.

Will Kyle Shanahan finally get his Super Bowl here in 2026? One of his former star receivers, Roddy White, doesn’t believe so, and also doesn’t ever see him winning a ring for a few reasons.

“No,” White said when asked about Shanahan winning a ring during his career on The Up And Adams Show. “They start like this every year. That team starts very fast every year. The only time they haven’t started fast is when they had everybody hurt. And this year they’re still managing to get people hurt, but they’re off to a good start. I think, me personally, that he’s a great offensive mind, right?

“But in tough situations, in pressure situations, the over-aggressive play calls always get him in trouble. And I think that’s just his mentality. He doesn’t play situational football well. That’s the only thing that I think that’s really like a knock on his game. And the thing that he does, he doesn’t play like situational football well. And that gets his team in trouble when you play against great quarterbacks. And when you make it to a Super Bowl, you’re gonna be playing against a great quarterback.”

The four-time Pro Bowl receiver for the Atlanta Falcons believes Shanahan has yet to learn game management and handling those situations in playoff games.

“Your ability to understand the flow of the game and the things like that is going to help you win those games,” White continued. “And I think especially if you have to play Patrick Mahomes in the Super Bowl. That guy has learned from Tom Brady, just playing him each and every year, playing him in Super Bowls. He knows what it takes. He can read what’s going on. He knows how to handle those situations, and he always comes out as a winner because he doesn’t give himself an opportunity to lose the game. And I think that Kyle always thinks about I have to win the game. I have to win the game instead of putting his players in the best position to win the game.

“He’s a great play caller, like great play caller. The play call sheet is deep. I will say that. But he seems to have a guy that can handle it. Being a part of that and just doing everything when Matt [Ryan] was there and going through everything. I mean, man, we’ll be on the sideline, and he’ll see something, boom, boom, boom. He’d be like, hey, man, I know we didn’t work this in practice, but it’s gonna work. Hey, this is what I want you to do. Boom, go out there, extra eye, execute the play, works. Boom, explosive play. So he’s very, very smart. I just think the aggressive play calling when not needed in pressure situations always gets the best of him.”

Shanahan’s game management, especially in go-for situations, had been one of the more scrutinized parts of him as a head coach earlier in his career. He had generally been too conservative in those situations and often went against analytics with his decisions. That has changed over the past few years, but White believes he’s gotten too aggressive as a play-caller.

So far this season, he’s been having a great year after arguably the best coaching season of his career in 2025 with a battered 49ers team. We’ll see if that can translate to postseason success, but the 49ers are putting themselves in a great spot to be successful in January with their start to the season.

item.title: CBS names J.J. Watt its No. 1 analyst beyond 2026
item.description: The upcoming game of broadcaster musical chairs has already begun.
item.content:encoded:
The upcoming game of broadcaster musical chairs has already begun. And one of the seats has already been filled.

CBS announced on Thursday morning that J.J. Watt will serve as the No. 1 NFL analyst beyond his one-year stint as Tony Romo's replacement.

Watt's "multi-year agreement" runs at least through next year's Super Bowl.

“I’ve had a front-row seat to JJ’s growth as a top-tier broadcaster, watching him tackle this role just like he did his hall-of-fame playing career,” Skydance Global Sports Group chairman David Berson said. “He’s insightful, entertaining, passionate, meticulous in his preparation, and the ultimate teammate. He has a unique ability to see things and communicate to fans of all levels. We are thrilled to have him leading our NFL coverage.”

Watt had been the No. 2 analyst at CBS until the network placed Romo on leave in August. CBS and Romo thereafter announced a permanent parting of ways.

The move takes off the table a potential destination for Troy Aikman, Greg Olsen, and others. For Aikman, the only viable spot could be Thursday Night Football. Prime Video has signed Kirk Herbstreit to a bird-in-the-hand extension, but it may not be as cheap to replace him after 2026 as previously reported.

That would leave only the Monday Night Football analyst job, if Aikman and ESPN don't find a way to mend fences. It's possible, frankly, that ESPN already knows who it will hire to replace Aikman. And if that's Greg Olsen, Aikman's only play could be to take the No. 2 spot at Fox — for considerably less than the $30 million annually he reportedly wanted from ESPN. Or the $18 million per year he's currently being paid.

Either way, CBS's decision to keep Watt takes one seat out of play for Aikman, Olsen, Travis Kelce, Sean McVay, or anyone else who may be looking for one of the highest-paying jobs in sports media.

item.title: Titans' JC Latham addresses Jordan Elliott gun incident: 'No bad blood'
item.description: Jordan Elliott attempted to confront JC Latham with a gun at Titans practice. The 23-year-old OT addressed the situation for the first time Oct. 21.
item.content:encoded:
Tennessee Titans offensive tackle JC Latham spoke on Wednesday, Oct. 21, for the first time since his former teammate, Jordan Elliott, was released from the team after attempting to confront him with a gun after a heated practice dispute.

Latham referred to the incident as "an unfortunate situation" while declining to provide many additional details about what happened.

"I mean, just heat of the moment, (expletive) happens," Latham told reporters. "So, there ain't really too much to say about it."

JC Latham, who was the source of Jordan Elliott’s frustration that led to the gun incident, speaks on the situation.Says they’d never had an argument before that. They were cool. Praying for him and sees it as a lapse of judgement. https://t.co/M7WH86TELY

— AtoZ Sports Nashville (@AtoZSports) October 21, 2026

The practice altercation between Elliott and Latham occurred on Thursday, Oct. 15, according to Aaron Wilson of KRPC Houston and Austin Stanley and Easton Freeze of AtoZSports.com.

Wilson reported that Elliott was told to leave the field after getting into it with Latham in practice. The defensive tackle reportedly removed his pads on the sideline, "stormed out" of the Titans' locker room and went to the players' parking lot to retrieve a gun from his car before Titans defensive tackle John Franklin-Myers stepped in to de-escalate the situation.

No one filed a report to the Metro Nashville Police Department, according to The Tennessean, part of the USA TODAY Network.

Titans coach Robert Saleh corroborated reports about what happened while also vouching for Elliott and expressing concerns about his mental health.

Latham acknowledged he was unaware of exactly what was happening while the situation unfolded, as he remained on the practice field after Elliott exited. The 23-year-old tackle expressed his appreciation for Franklin-Myers' intervention while also saying he would reach out to Elliott if granted the opportunity.

"It ain’t never been no bad blood between us two," Latham said about his relationship with Elliott. "We were here over the summer getting treatment before that. We hung out whenever we were in the same city together. We actually never had an argument leading up to it."

"I do think mental health is important," Latham added. "That’s just one of those situations where you pray for a guy like that, and if you can, reach out for him. Hope for the best for him. But it’s no bad blood. It's nothing personal on my end."

USA TODAY Sports' Jack McKessy also contributed to this report.
