item.title: Where on Earth was Brandon Cisse going?
item.description: In the new Madden ratings, Cisse will be getting a zero for ball carrier vision.
item.content:encoded:
What on earth. Where on earth. How on earth. Why on earth. It may not technically be the worst interception return in the history of football, but Brandon Cisse’s run on Sunday night against the Dallas Cowboys must have one of the worst ratios of distance covered to yardage gained.

The Green Bay Packers’ rookie cornerback got his first NFL interception last weekend, but it was an absurd run after he made the catch. Cisse initially catches the ball on the numbers at the twenty yard line. On an NFL field the numbers are approximately forty yards away from the opposite sideline. Cisse ends up returning the ball all the way to the twenty three yard line. That’s a 40:3 ratio at best. Even MarShawn Lloyd finds that inefficient.

When Cisse first looks up after securing the catch, here is the picture he sees.

There are two opposing receivers as immediate tacklers. The intended receiver, CeeDee Lamb, has been blocked and is about to get double-teamed as Zaire Franklin is approaching. Rather than running away from the pursuing receiver across the middle of the field and following a potential lead blocker in a race against the collective Dallas Cowboys’ offensive line and Dak Prescott, Cisse decides to immediately go against the grain and cut behind the pursuing player. This is the worst choice.

It’s a split-second choice, but Cisse has a worse angle on the greatest number of Cowboys here. The entire offensive line is more medial to the field than he is, and there are multiple receivers whom have the speed to chase him on that side of the field. On his current side of the field, the only threat is about to be double-teamed, and Cisse has an opportunity to press his physical advantage towards the near sideline where both his current lead blockers and also the defensive line can either clear a path or create enough chaos to make a crease. As we saw on the almost-pick-six from Dallas earlier in the game, offensive lines and quarterbacks are terrible tacklers. You have to challenge them to stop you.

Look at it. After dispatching with the pursuing Jake Ferguson, Cisse finds himself in a very advantageous position now. The offensive line committed to the near sideline, and now he has a chance to press the angle towards the far sideline but start picking up yardage. Keisean Nixon will have to be careful not to get a blindside blocking foul and do an airplane block, but between him and Xavier McKinney, Cisse will have blockers who can take care of both wide receivers on that side of the field. Then it’s down to Cisse, Dak Prescott, and the Cowboys protection unit.

Instead Cisse bounces it and ends up in a situation where he has no blocker for the receiver on the far sideline, and ends up just taking it out of bounds. That’s a lot of effort for three to four yards, and it’s not exactly an elite display of ball carrier vision. Hopefully we see Cisse get many more opportunities this year to work out the kinks.

item.title: 13 NFL coordinators under most pressure to turn things around
item.description: There haven't been any significant firings in the NFL coaching ranks this season, but these 13 coordinators are under pressure as midseason nears.
item.content:encoded:
Through six weeks, the NFL hasn't had a firing at the top coaching levels.

That period of quiet, however, might not extend much longer.

As the league approaches its midseason point, several head coaches find themselves firmly on the hot seat. But with many teams still harboring hopes of mounting a push that will put them right back into the playoff hunt, immediate action to topple an entire power structure might not be imminent.

Yet it could be a different story at the coordinator level, where teams typically are less reserved about making a change during the season. And while there haven't been any full dismissals yet, two coordinators – the Houston Texans' Matt Burke (defense) and Denver Broncos' Davis Webb (offense) – have already had their respective head coaches strip them of their play-calling duties.

Regardless of whether their jobs are in jeopardy, here are 13 NFL coordinators under the most pressure to reverse their early-season trend lines:

Arizona Cardinals defensive coordinator Nick Rallis

A stark turnaround in an 18-16 win over the Rams likely lowered the temperature on Rallis considerably. Still, the holdover from Jonathan Gannon's coaching staff can't let that performance be an outlier. No other team has allowed more points per game than Arizona (29.7), which also has ranked among the league's least efficient units in generating pressure. But Rallis wisely pivoted from his previous reliance on four-man rushes and unleashed a bevy of blitzes against the Rams to great effect. A similar approach might be required to prop up a group that's still short on top talent on that side of the ball.

Buffalo Bills defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard

Unlike some others on this list, Leonhard probably isn't facing questions of job security as he oversees a fairly significant shift in adapting former coach Sean McDermott's defense to a radically different scheme. But with Buffalo otherwise looking capable of competing for its first title, he's hardly off the hook.

The Bills have raced to a 5-1 start despite giving up 29 or more points in all but one of their first six games. Weekly shootouts surely aren't what was envisioned by Leonhard, who came over after helping the Denver Broncos become one of the league's most stifling units the last two years. But with the defense liable to give up big gains whenever edge rusher Greg Rousseau or defensive tackle Deone Walker don't create sufficient disruption, Buffalo's defense has made for a wild ride. There might be only so much that Leonhard can do to cover for a glaring problem at corner and other holes, but this might be the greatest impediment to a Josh Allen Super Bowl run if left unaddressed.

Dallas Cowboys defensive coordinator Christian Parker

With Brian Schottenheimer's offense weighing Dallas down the last two weeks, Parker is no longer the sole target of scorn on the Cowboys' coaching staff. Still, things seem mighty unsettled for a defensive play-caller who only needed to bring about modest progress to be considered successful in Year 1.

It's easy to see why Jerry Jones and Co. sought to bring Mike Pettine out of retirement as additional support for Parker. Dallas ranks 31st in defensive EPA per play (+0.12) while sitting last for defensive EPA per dropback (+0.28) and rushing yards per game (149.8). At least the move to bring on Pettine seems like a sincere attempt to aid Parker rather than a warning shot to him. And with the Cowboys having a healthier roster than any of its NFC East foes and a schedule that serves up five teams with losing records in the next six contests, there's reason to believe that better days are ahead. But if Dallas can't box in a severely shorthanded Eagles attack, things could get dire in a hurry.

Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard

There's nowhere to hide for a Detroit defense that, even after a promising performance against the Cardinals, ranks last in yards allowed per game (404.4, nearly 20 more than the next closest team) and defensive EPA/play (+0.13). A good portion of the Lions' woes can be attributed to personnel shortcomings, particularly in a woefully undermanned secondary. Still, even though Sheppard said it was insulting to suggest his unit was being carried by the offense, how else would you explain the Lions' results this season besides pointing to the disparity between the two groups?

Lions coach Dan Campbell has tried to take the focus away from the defense, saying that all parts of the operation can stand to improve. Even if he ends up being given a good deal more grace than others on this list, Sheppard has to start conjuring solutions for a team at risk of squandering a fifth consecutive season with a top-five offense in both yardage and scoring. Bracketing Cardinals tight end Trey McBride and wide receiver Michael Wilson to keep both in check was a good first step. Still, ultra-versatile safety Brian Branch's season debut comes at a critical time, with Detroit challenged to slow down the Green Bay Packers' explosive downfield passing attack.

Indianapolis Colts defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo

While Colts coach Shane Steichen appears safe for the time, owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon put everyone in Indianapolis on notice this week with the firing of general manager Chris Ballard. Change is afoot for an organization that earlier this year seemed committed to the status quo, and it's hard to imagine the upheaval will stop at Ballard's dismissal.

One year after Anarumo's complex coverages and simulated pressures had opponents turned around, the Colts' defense now only seems to be confounding itself. Missed tackles have become a fixture of the unit, with its vulnerabilities at the second level and over the middle becoming even more pronounced. Indianapolis ranks last in rushing EPA/play allowed (+0.05), per Next Gen Stats. And with a league-worst pressure rate of 24.4% and just three takeaways, the defense has been just as bad at generating splash plays as it has been at preventing them. Defensive tackle and team captain DeForest Buckner's declaration that he was "sick and tired of the same song and dance every year" after a loss to the Titans was a rough look for the team. But it's likely that sentiment is shared by some decision-makers who probably will try to take corrective action on that trajectory.

Los Angeles Chargers offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel

What's left to say about an outfit that rapidly separated itself as the biggest disappointment in the league? The Charges are dead last in EPA per play (-0.26), while Justin Herbert has thrown a league-worst eight interceptions.

At this point, it's almost impossible to envision the Bolts becoming the scintillating scoring machine many foresaw when McDaniel was first hired. The search for mere functionality might point Jim Harbaugh toward streamlining what's long been understood as a fairly intricate scheme that can require extensive time to click. But Harbaugh's shifting tone, from backing McDaniel without reservation after Week 4 to saying he would "evaluate every part of what we're doing," underscores the depths of the Chargers' discontent. Cleaning up the incessant penalties and stabilizing the protection should be the short-term priorities, but a fundamentally broken operation might not be fixable on the fly.

Los Angeles Rams special teams coordinator Bubba Ventrone

Amid yet another special teams meltdown, Sean McVay made explicit that he wouldn't jettison Ventrone, saying last week that he has "a lot of confidence" in the coordinator and that "there’s no changes that are gonna be made there." Given that last December's firing of special teams coordinator Chase Blackburn did little to stop a late-season downturn, staying the course with the staff might be a necessary step for an otherwise volatile unit. After Harrison Mevis was cut and replacement Blake Grupe suffered a torn anterior cruciate ligament in his first game with the team, Los Angeles is looking to Brandon McManus to stem its kicking woes.

Ventrone might not bear responsibility for the injury to Grupe that necessitated a third kicker in as many weeks, but he is culpable for a unit that has converted a league-worst 60% of its field goals. And the Rams' struggles to handle their own kickoff coverage as well as create a spark on their own returns have reflected poorly on Ventrone, with the team ranking 29th in average starting field position and 30th in opponents' average starting field position. There's still plenty of time for repairs, but this underperforming cohort can't afford many more slip-ups on this front.

New Orleans Saints defensive coordinator Brandon Staley

Typically reserved team owner Gayle Benson took everyone within the organization to task last week, saying fans were "right to expect more than we have delivered." Staley's defense responded by New York Giants backup quarterback J.J. McCarthy to engineer three fourth-quarter scoring drives, bringing his team to the precipice of a nearly unfathomable comeback before falling just short in a 34-27 New Orleans victory. At least the first three quarters of that game should give some confidence to a group that, after exceeding expectations in Staley's inaugural season at the helm, has come unglued at times in 2026. With no consistent top performers outside of edge rusher Chase Young, New Orleans' defense sits tied for last in points allowed per game (29.7). Just as the offense needs more splash plays, Staley's crew also might have to count on big swings after four takeaways proved integral to the win over the Giants. Failing that, however, New Orleans might continue to have difficulty generating consistent stops.

New York Jets offensive coordinator Frank Reich

The 64-year-old didn't make it to the end of the season in either of his previous two pro coaching posts. Seems fair to question whether that trend will hold yet again.

Aaron Glenn issued the obligatory vote of confidence last week for Reich, who has helped the offense avoid the rampant setbacks that plagued last year's unit. Yet any sense of efficiency has been consistently undermined by an inability to deliver in crunch time, particularly in the red zone, where the Jets rank last in touchdown rate, and in two-minute scenarios. A light schedule the next two weeks – at home against the Dolphins and Raiders – should provide an opportunity to pick things up before midseason, but there don't seem like many sources capable of pushing this unit forward.

Philadelphia Eagles offensive coordinator Sean Mannion

There might not be a play-caller throughout the NFL in a deeper early-season hole than the one Mannion finds himself in. Between an all-new backfield and front that featured three fill-ins, the offensive lineup that the Eagles trotted out against the Carolina Panthers in Week 6 was almost unrecognizable from the one that the coordinator first envisioned carrying out his scheme.

But with Tanner McKee in line to hold down the rest of the season in place of Jalen Hurts, Mannion appears to be an impasse. A scheme rooted in being under center and emphasizing play-action looks doesn't suit the fourth-year signal-caller's skill set. That could prompt Mannion to abandon much of what he was counting on to resuscitate this attack. But doing so would essentially leave him with no proof of concept for how this offense should operate under better circumstances. Getting Saquon Barkley back from a hamstring injury should at least boost a ground game that has seen rushing attempts stuffed at or behind the line of scrimmage on nearly a quarter of the team's carries, according to Next Gen Stats. That's about the only reason for optimism to be found for Philadelphia's offense, though.

Seattle Seahawks offensive coordinator Brian Fleury

Following in Klint Kubiak's footsteps was always going to be an exceedingly difficult task, even as Fleury maintained he intended to maintain as much of his predecessor's framework as possible. In his first season as a play-caller, however, Fleury is experiencing many of the challenges Kubiak encountered while having far fewer avenues for relief.

The inefficiency of the run game is once again the primary culprit for Seattle's problems. But while Sam Darnold picked up the slack early last year to keep things afloat until the rushing attack took off late in the regular season and into the playoffs, the quarterback has come unglued this fall, throwing seven interceptions in his four games since returning from a glute injury. The issue came to a head last week, when Darnold's two late interceptions doomed the team in a 17-14 overtime loss to the Denver Broncos. With Zach Charbonnet on track to make his season debut after tearing his anterior cruciate ligament in January and first-round rookie Jadarian Price potentially joining him with a return in the near future, Seattle could finally strike the offensive balance necessary to create some sense of harmony. But Darnold also has to be more decisive and attack the intermediate area more efficiently to avoid the sacks and interceptions that are proving insurmountable for the unit.

Tampa Bay Buccaneers offensive coordinator Zac Robinson

Having an undrafted free agent take over at quarterback might typically buy an offensive coordinator a reprieve. But outside of a surprising outing against the Cowboys that scored the team its lone win so far, Robinson hasn't done much with either Jalon Daniels or Baker Mayfield to help his own cause.

While Bucky Irving has enjoyed a resurgent campaign, Tampa Bay's offense can't claim to do many things well consistently. Turnovers have compounded the team's troubles with holding onto late leads, with Daniels' two fourth-quarter interceptions factoring heavily into a 26-19 overtime loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers. With Bowles seemingly on the hot seat himself in his fifth year, executing a midseason change might be difficult unless things truly reach a breaking point. Regardless, unless Robinson can coax high-level play out of Mayfield upon the quarterback's return, don't expect much stability from a franchise that's now on its fifth different play-caller of Bowles' tenure.

Tennessee Titans offensive coordinator Brian Daboll

Notching their first win of the season might have spared the Titans from scrutiny for a week, but even the 26-20 victory over the Colts didn't reflect well on Daboll or his offense. Tennessee netted just 186 yards on a day in which its defense and special teams did most of the heavy lifting.

Nearly all of the numbers are foreboding for the Titans, who rank last in yards per game (236.3) and are tied for 31st in scoring (14 points per game). Yet in Year 1 of Robert Saleh's reset, the development of 2025 No. 1 pick Cam Ward might be the better reflection of Daboll's value rather than the overall health of the offense. The early returns haven't been favorable to either the coordinator or the quarterback, the latter of whom has largely looked erratic and unsettled. While Ward's supporting cast hasn't equipped him with nearly enough help, both the quarterback and Daboll still have work to do to demonstrate they deserve to be seen as long-term solutions for the franchise.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: 13 NFL coordinators under most pressure to turn things around

item.title: Caleb Williams Week 6 QB Grade: Bears @ Falcons Film Breakdown
item.description: A deeper look with @iamcogs at Caleb Willaims and the Chicago Bears’ 31-23 bounce back victory against the Falcons.
item.content:encoded:
Well, that was a pretty nice way to welcome Caleb Williams back.

After missing three games with the hamstring injury he suffered against Minnesota, Williams returned to the lineup Sunday in Atlanta and looked about as sharp as you could reasonably ask for in his first live action in nearly a month.

Chicago jumped out to a 14-0 lead on its first two possessions, with Williams completing all 10 of his passes for 122 yards and a touchdown on those drives. He eventually connected on his first 12 attempts, the longest streak of his career, and the Bears never trailed in a 31-23 win that moved them to 4-2.

Williams finished 30-of-36 for 305 yards, one touchdown and no interceptions, good for a 111.2 passer rating.

That 83.3% completion rate wasn’t just a career high. It was the highest completion percentage by a Bears quarterback in franchise history on 30 or more attempts, breaking a record previously shared by Mitchell Trubisky, Shane Matthews and Steve Walsh.

And the accuracy gets even more ridiculous when you dig a little deeper.

ESPN Insights charted Williams at 26-of-26 for 255 yards when Atlanta failed to pressure him, the most unpressured attempts without an incompletion since ESPN began tracking pressure in 2009. Next Gen Stats came to a similar conclusion using its clean-pocket definition, tracking him at 24-of-24 for 248 yards, the most clean-pocket attempts without an incompletion in a game since at least 2018.

Pretty good for a guy coming off a hamstring injury.

What I liked most, though, was how Williams got to those numbers.

His 3.6-yard average depth of target was the second-lowest of his career, so this wasn’t Williams spending the afternoon bombing the ball downfield. Instead, he consistently took what Atlanta gave him when they committed to playing two high safeties most of the afternoon. Williams responded by getting the football into the hands of his playmakers and trusting them to create after the catch.

Press Taylor summed it up nicely afterward, saying Williams did a good job taking what the defense gave him and avoiding forced throws. That’s an important part of the growth we’ve been looking for. Williams has always possessed the ability to turn chaos into something spectacular, but sometimes the best answer is simply taking the completion and moving on to the next snap.

But all that doesn’t mean the aggressive throws disappeared either.

When Atlanta presented opportunities downfield, Williams still took them. There was a 22-yard strike to Luther Burden III, and one of his best throws of the afternoon came on a 23-yard completion to Rome Odunze, where Williams worked through the coverage and ripped the dig route to move the chains on 3rd and 17. And not to mention his touchdown to Colston Loveland, a throw that maybe your only comfortable seeing 3 or 4 other QB’s in the league try.

In other words, the lower aDOT wasn’t Williams refusing to push the football downfield. It was Williams choosing when to. He said essentially the same thing afterward: almost every pass concept has a shot available somewhere, but if the defense takes it away, get the ball to the underneath option and let your guys go make a play. That’s the balance you want to see.

The performance also put Williams into some pretty elite company.

His opening-drive touchdown to Colston Loveland gave him 50 career touchdown passes before throwing his 15th interception. Williams became just the third quarterback in NFL history to accomplish that, joining Patrick Mahomes and Lamar Jackson. Both, of course, former MVP’s.

Sunday was also Williams’ fifth career game with at least 300 passing yards and no interceptions, breaking Brian Hoyer’s Bears franchise record.

And apparently the NFL thought the afternoon was pretty good too.

Williams was named NFC Offensive Player of the Week, the second time he’s earned the award in his career. That ties Jay Cutler for the most Player of the Week awards by a Bears quarterback in team history.

Caleb wasn’t the only Bear making his return felt, either.

Kyler Gordon made his season debut after missing the first five games and somehow managed to record three sacks and two forced fumbles despite playing a limited defensive role on 16 total snaps. According to Novig, Gordon became the first defensive back in the last 40 seasons to record at least three sacks and multiple forced fumbles in the same game.

His final sack couldn’t have come at a better time.

After Chicago built a 31-7 lead, Atlanta scored 16 unanswered points to suddenly make things far more interesting than they had any business being. Gordon ended the threat with a strip-sack of Michael Penix Jr. with 2:54 remaining, allowing Devin Bush to recover the football and the Bears to finally put the game away.

It wasn’t a completely flawless afternoon. Williams took four sacks, the Bears committed 12 penalties for 133 yards and what looked like a blowout became uncomfortable late.

But after watching the offense completely unravel at Lambeau one week earlier, Williams’ return was a pretty emphatic reminder of the difference he makes.

The explosive, off-script plays will always be part of what makes Caleb special. Sunday showed that he doesn’t necessarily need them to dominate a football game.

Now let’s get into the numbers.

Benchmarks

(Season totals are underlined, Season Averages in Italics, and this week’s stats appear in regular text.)

C/A:36/55 (65.5%) | 18/27.5 (65.5%) | 30/36 83.3%

Yards:407 | 203.5 | 305

Touchdowns: 4 | 2 | 1

Turnovers: 1| 0.5 | 0

QB at Fault Sacks:0 |0| 1

aDOT:7.7 | 3.6

Passer Rating: 92.0 | 111.2

True Passer Rating:113.4 | 106.5

Time to Throw:3.34s | 3.08s

Time to Pressure:2.75s | 2.25s

Pressure Rate:41.57% | 33.33%

On-Target Rate:83.3% | 88.9%

Poor Play Rate / Big Play Rate: 7.5% PPR / 5.0% BRP | 2.1% PPR / 6.3% BRP

EPA per dropback:+0.31 | +0.25

ANY/A:6.2 | 7.3

Game Scorecard

The full grading sheet for each play can be found here.

Game Notes

Note: Last year, I included PFF grades in these breakdowns. With PFF continuing to expand its use of AI across its platform, and with my confidence in how accurately its grades reflect quarterback performance declining, I’ve decided to move away from them this season. In their place, I’ll be using PFN’s Impact Score, which will be notated as PFN on grading sheets moving forward.

NFL Passer Rating / True Passer Rating / PFN Impact Score: 111.2 / 106.5 / 80.5

  • The NFL’s average passer rating through Week 6 sits at 91.0, making Williams’ 111.2 against Atlanta a very good mark that pushes toward elite territory.
  • A 106.5 TPR lands slightly above the 100-point baseline for “Average.”
    • TPR’s aDOT component works as a sliding scale around 7.0 yards, with very conservative passing pulling the score down and more aggressive depth creating additional value. Williams’ low aDOT cost him some points here, while his accuracy and overall efficiency were enough to keep the final score comfortably above average.
    • His 106.5 TPR finished 6.5 points above the model’s average baseline and 12.5 points above the 2025 league-average TPR of 94.0.
  • On the PFN scale, where 75 represents an average qualifying starter and 90 is elite territory, Williams finished Week 6 with an 80.5 Impact Score, good for 4th best in week 6 behind just C.J. Stroud (82.6), J.J. McCarthy (82.3), and Trevor Lawrence (81.1).

On-Target Throws: 2026 Average: 83.3% | Week 6: 88.9%

  • Reminder: Completion percentage ≠ On-Target Percentage. I only chart aimed passes, meaning throwaways, spikes and passes deflected at the line are excluded. Drops can still be credited as on-target.
  • Short-Level Passing (Behind LOS–9 yards): 27/28 | 96.4% On-Target
  • Deep-Level Passing (10+ Yards Downfield): 5/8 | 62.5% On-Target
    • Three games played, three On-Target rates north of 80%. Williams accomplished that just once over the entirety of the 2025 season.
    • While most of his game took place under 10 yards, he still hit on a respectable rate beyond 10-yards, with nice completions to Rome Odunze, Colston Loveland, and Luther Burden.
    • It might go without saying but his 96.4% on target % in the short-level set a career high mark.

Poor Play Rate / Big Play Rate: 2.1% PPR / 6.3% BPR

  • On the season, Williams now sits at a 3.9% Poor Play Rate and 7.0% Big Play Rate.
    • His BPR is right around his 2025 season average of 7.6%.
    • The much bigger development has been the reduction in poorly graded plays. Williams finished 2025 at 9.0% and currently sits at 3.9%, a decrease of 5.1 percentage points.
  • His lone poorly graded play against Atlanta came on a pass intended for D’Andre Swift that was nearly intercepted.
    • The play still receives a grade despite the penalty because it was committed by the offense. Had the defender secured the interception, Atlanta could have declined the penalty and taken possession.

EPA per Dropback: 2026 Average: +0.29 | Week 6: +0.25

  • Williams landed almost directly on his season average in EPA/dropback.
    • For some added context, a +0.25 mark would have been his fourth-best single-game result of 2025, trailing only Dallas (+0.80), San Francisco (+0.39) and Cincinnati (+0.38).

What’s the deal with aDOT?

  • In Williams’ last two starts, his aDOT has hovered around four yards or lower. Naturally, some people have grabbed onto that and labeled him a “checkdown merchant,” despite many of those same people spending much of 2025 arguing that he needed to operate within structure and take what the defense gave him more often.
    • Two games is an incredibly small sample in the context of an NFL season. More importantly, it doesn’t really match Williams’ established profile. His aDOT sat at 8.1 yards in 2024 and climbed to 8.9 in 2025, clearly establishing him as a quarterback willing to attack downfield.
    • The recent context matters too. One of those games came in miserable weather against Brian Flores and an historically aggressive Minnesota defense. The other ended with Williams throwing for 305 yards at 8.5 yards per attempt while completing 83.3% of his passes.
    • A two-game stretch of shorter throws doesn’t suddenly erase two full seasons showing a willingness to push the football downfield.

The Irony of Context:

  • The funny part of the entire aDOT conversation is that short-area accuracy was actually one of Williams’ weaknesses in 2025. He finished that season with just a 73.5% On-Target rate on throws between 1 and 9 yards.
    • The sample is obviously smaller this year, but the early returns have been dramatically better. Williams currently sits at 92.5% On-Target on short-level throws, connecting accurately on 37 of 40 attempts.
    • Among the six quarterbacks I’m grading this season, Williams currently leads the group in play-action On-Target rate (87.0%), Behind-LOS On-Target rate (100.0%), short-level On-Target rate (92.5%), mid-level On-Target rate (72.7%) and overall On-Target rate (85.4%).
    • The only level where he doesn’t rank first is deep passing, where his 42.9% On-Target rate currently ranks second.

Understated and Underrated: Pre-snap Processing

  • The film was littered with examples of Williams making calls at the line, adjusting protections, killing plays and generally commanding the pre-snap chess match based on what Atlanta presented. This is an important developmental step, and one where plenty of young quarterbacks can get stonewalled. More often than not, though, Williams is identifying the look correctly, getting the offense into the right play and shifting protections where they need to go. We’re starting to see him move beyond simply executing the offense and toward actually commanding it. When Ben Johnson said Williams was well ahead of everyone when it comes to the terms of this offense back in spring, that sentiment shows up between the downs on film.

Play Reviews

The plays we’ll be reviewing are presented in the order they occurred in the game.

Situation: 1st Quarter, 2nd and 13 ATL13 08:25
Play Grade: Elite
Result: 14-yard touchdown to Colston Loveland
Notes: (+) Positive Play Extension (+) Touch/Layering (++) Difficulty of Throw (+++) Mid-Level Accuracy/Ball Placement

Analysis: We start with the first touchdown of the game, where Caleb found Loveland with a exceptional ball after extending the play.

The Bears threaten the middle here with Loveland releasing up the inside seam and Raymond running a post outside him, while Kmet works toward the flat underneath. The initial routes don’t give the quarterback an immediate completion, mainly due to the pocket compressing before they are finished.

The escape to his right keeps the play alive. He maintains his eyes downfield and stays in position to throw, giving Loveland time to adjust and work across toward the goal line, flowing with his Quarterback. That movement creates a new opportunity after the original timing of the play has passed.

Delivering the ball while moving makes this difficult enough, but the placement is what elevates it. The quarterback has to clear the underneath defender without carrying the pass into the coverage beyond Loveland. He drops it into that narrow space, reaching Loveland’s extended hands near the goal line before the closing defender can break it up.

Loveland secures the pass through contact and finishes into the end zone for the fourteen-yard touchdown. The extension creates the chance, and an exceptionally difficult, precise throw finishes it. This play showcases exactly why Caleb is a high ceiling quarterback.

Situation: 1st Quarter, 3rd and 17 CHI34 05:15
Play Grade: Great
Result: 23-yard completion to Rome Odunze
Notes: (+) Anticipation (+) Explosive Play (+) Mid-Level Accuracy/Completion (+) Long 3rd Down Conversion

Analysis: Our next play the Bears are facing a 3rd and 17, for most quarterbacks and offenses this is a death sentence to a drive.

Not the Bears.

In what has become a staple of the Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams led offense, Odunze runs a deep dig from the bottom of the screen, while the trips side sends routes vertically and across the field. The post paired with Rome’s dig gives this a Mills-style relationship across the formation, stretching the deep coverage while Rome breaks underneath it.

Caleb begins his delivery before Odunze has fully turned across the field. Rome still has a defender close behind him, so waiting for obvious separation would give that defender more time to recognize the break. Instead, the ball is already traveling as Rome works into the window of the throw.

For the depth of the throw, the ball placement is acceptable but is worth noting it causes Rome to leave his feet, which muddies up any potential huge gain involving YAC since it allows the trailing defender to close.

However it’s a chunk play that turns a difficult third-and-long into a twenty-three-yard completion and a fresh set of downs. The anticipation creates the opportunity, and the accuracy allows Rome to finish with coverage still close enough to contest the catch.

Situation: 1st Quarter, 1st and 10 ATL43 04:28
Play Grade: Good
Result: 25-yard completion to Luther Burden III
Notes: (+) Anticipation (+) Mid-Level Accuracy/Completion (+) Explosive Play

Analysis: Play 3 (and 3rd throw in a row) showcases a nice anticipation ball from Caleb setting up a YAC opportunity for Luther Burden.

Burden does a great job creating this opportunity by selling the go route at the bottom of the screen. The corner retreats to protect against the deep ball, Burden then throttles down and works back toward the quarterback. On the opposite side, Odunze pushes vertically running a mirrored route while Kmet releases underneath toward the flat, giving the offense options at different depths.

Williams starts his delivery before Burden had fully throttled down. He recognizes the cushion and throws into the space underneath the corner, trusting Burden to come back to the ball. That anticipation helps preserve the separation Burden creates with his change of direction.

The pass reaches Burden in that window perfectly. He turns up field before the corner can close, then breaks a tackle from the corner immediately after. It’s an accurate intermediate completion made possible by Williams trusting his timing with his WR. Burden’s elite YAC ability turns it into an explosive twenty-five-yard thanks to this mutual trust.

Situation: 3rd Quarter, 1st and 10 CHI48 04:28
Play Grade: Great
Result: 22-yard completion to Luther Burden III
Notes: (+) Anticipation (+) Explosive Play (+) Touch/Layering (+) Mid-Level Accuracy/Completion

Analysis: We skip to the 3rd quarter, after the Falcons adjusted early to the Bears attacking deep, Williams and company were more than happy to take what the Falcons were leaving underneath, but that doesn’t mean when an opportunity hit’s the pass it up.

This completion is a perfect example of that.

The Bears run a flood switch concept here, attacking the right side of the field at three depths. The outside route stretches the coverage downfield, Burden breaks toward the sideline on the intermediate corner route, and Raymond works into the flat underneath. That spacing puts the underneath defender in conflict while creating a window behind him for Burden.

The quarterback commits to the throw before Burden reaches that window, showing good anticipation once more. With the underneath defender dropping into the throwing lane and deeper coverage closing from outside, waiting for obvious separation would give the defense time to squeeze the route, putting the ball in a potentially dangerous position.

The pass clears the underneath defender and drops toward Burden before the deeper defender can get across to break it up. That’s where the touch and layering show up. Burden extends vertically to secure the ball, then holds on through the arriving contact for a twenty-two-yard completion. This play just misses out on being an Elite level throw due to it Caleb being just a tick late and high.

This throw would ultimately led to a Roshon Johnson 4-yard touchdown run, and a 28-7 Bears lead.

Summary

Caleb Williams finishes Week 6 with final grades of 1st Half (2.50) / 2nd Half (1.60) / Game (4.10), which is a few points into a “Good” start.

This gives Williams 2 Good or better starts in his three starts this year, the only outlier being the Week 2 Vikings game where he scored an “Average” grade of 1.55, an extremely solid start to the season thus far for the third year QB looking to take the next leap as this franchises’ Quarterback.

After missing three weeks with a hamstring injury, it would’ve been understandable if Williams needed some time to knock off the rust.

Instead, he came back and delivered one of the cleanest performances we’ve seen from him.

The 83.3% completion percentage speaks for itself, but I think the more encouraging part was how he got there. Williams wasn’t constantly hunting for the spectacular play. He took what Atlanta gave him, consistently put the football where it needed to be and trusted his playmakers to create after the catch. When opportunities opened farther downfield, he still showed the willingness and arm talent to take advantage of them.

That’s the balance a lot of us have wanted to see.

The low aDOT will understandably stand out, especially after a similar number against Minnesota, but two games don’t suddenly redefine the type of quarterback Williams has been throughout his career. If anything, Sunday showed another way he can successfully attack a defense.

He finished with just one poorly graded play, maintained an 88.9% On-Target rate and still generated enough high-end throws to finish with a positive Big Play Rate. Coming off an injury and three weeks without game action, that’s a pretty encouraging way to return.

Of the six quarterbacks I’m grading this season, you can see where Williams’ Week 6 performance landed among the group here. For a look at how the entire group stacks up through six weeks, along with some notes on the other quarterbacks from this week’s slate, you can find that here.

And there won’t be much time to enjoy this one.

The Bears return home on a short week to host the New England Patriots just a handful of hours from now on Thursday Night Football. After three weeks wondering when QB1 would return, it’s nice to finally get back to evaluating Caleb Williams every week.

Until next week, Bear Down!

Gary Baugher Jr. is a second year contributor to WCG, bringing football insight backed by over 16 years of experience in organized football and more than 30 years as a passionate fan of the game. You can follow him on Twitter at @iamcogs.

item.title: Read & React: Are the young Steelers living up to their new money?
item.description: Pittsburgh gave new money to the middle three selections of their 2023 draft class… and sent away their top two picks.
item.content:encoded:
With the win last Sunday against the Buccaneers, the Steelers wrapped up the first third of the NFL season 4-2. While there is still plenty of game action left in the season, it does feel like a checkpoint where we can do our first check-in on one of the biggest storylines of the Steelers’ 2026 offseason: which young members of the 2023 draft class the organization would commit to long-term.

The 2023 draft class was the first group selected by the tandem of general manager Omar Khan and assistant general manager Andy Weidl. While both were in place for the 2022 season, the Steelers made the unusual move of having retiring general manager Kevin Colbert stick it out through the draft process before hanging it up. That meant this offseason was the new duo’s first time attempting to decide which of their personally selected homegrown talents would remain in their plans, and which would not.

They ultimately decided that three players — outside linebacker Nick Herbig (four years, $100 million), defensive tackle Keeanu Benton (four years, $72 million), and tight end Darnell Washington (four years, $42 million) — were worthy and willing enough to accept an extension. Meanwhile, two others — cornerback Joey Porter Jr. and tackle Broderick Jones — were not able to do the same.

We don’t need to relitigate why Porter Jr. and Jones are no longer Steelers. Jones will go down as a misstep from Khan and Weidl’s first draft. How the Porter Jr. decision will be remembered is slightly more complicated. The way we’ll talk about his departure in the coming years will depend partially on how Porter performs post-Pittsburgh. It’s also hard to make any definitive claims about how this decision will affect the franchise in the long term until we see how Pittsburgh addresses the cornerback position this spring, as well as how they spend the second-round pick from his trade package when they finally get to use it in 2028. Regardless, it’s a disappointing outcome for two players who once held so much promise for the team.

In deciding to pay Herbig, Benton, and Washington, but not Porter, the Steelers have once again affirmed that they value building in the trenches. For two straight years, they have dispensed with players who play more in the boundaries of the field — last year it was wide receiver George Pickens — and looked to retool those positions in the draft and free agency. Certainly, there were indeed other factors at play in the decision to let both of those players go, but it is revealing about the team’s priorities, nonetheless.

This week, we’ll be looking at the players from the 2023 class the organization did commit to. While none of them have started to receive that new money on the books just yet, we’ll try to determine if they’re still trending in the right direction in terms of development. We’ll be taking their entire seasons thus far into account, but will be looking closely at the most recent game against Tampa Bay with this week’s film study.

Let’s dive in.

Nick Herbig

New deal total: 4 years, $100 million (10th among edge rushers)

AAV: $25 million (11th)

Guaranteed money at signing: $21 million (29th)

RB: After failing to record a sack in the first five games of 2026, Herbig logged two against Tampa Bay last week – in arguably the toughest assignment of his season thus far with most of his snaps coming against All-Pro tackle Tristain Wirfs. 

While I certainly wasn’t shocked to see Herbig get the big contract he did this offseason, it felt like one that was paying for future usage more than past output. But don’t get me wrong: Herbig has been ridiculously efficient during his past seasons as a Steeler, logging a 7.5 sack season in 2025, good for second-best on the team. 

The impressive part was that Herbig put up those numbers playing just 59.6% of the Steelers’ defensive snaps in 2025 – a number that was only as high as it was due to both TJ Watt and Alex Highsmith missing some games. While Herbig was undoubtedly worth $25 million per year as a pass rusher, could the Steelers justify paying him that with both Watt and Highsmith still under contract, and with Herbig still losing snaps to both? 

Of course, that’s not an entirely fair way to frame things: As Ryan mentioned in the intro, Herbig’s new-contract cap hit won’t kick in until 2027 (it jumps from $5.4 million to $25.2 million), meaning that the Steelers won’t really have a dilemma about paying too many good edge rushers until next year. 

But at the same time, the Steelers made a big commitment to Herbig, and in 2026 he’s played just 54.3% of the team’s defensive snaps (and still 37% of the team’s special teams snaps) and saw his efficiency numbers drop with a 10.2% pressure rate through six games – on pace for the worst of his career by over four percentage points. 

While only pass rush snaps count towards pressure rate, it is fair to point out that Herbig has had far more varied usage in Patrick Graham’s defense, with 63 of his 138 snaps so far this season coming at positions other than edge — something he’s admitted has been a challenge. Herbig has been playing off-ball linebacker more and rushing everywhere from over guards to being lined up in the slot. And in a new defense with a higher emphasis on simulated pressures and stunts, not every snap is designed for Herbig to get home to the quarterback, either. 

According to NFL Pro, Herbig is only averaging 14.7 pass rush snaps per game, down from 21.9 last year. 

Still, Pittsburgh paid Herbig as a pass rusher, and the team’s usage of him – and his production – hasn’t entirely reflected that yet. 

But against Tampa Bay on Sunday, Herbig showed any doubters that the speed rusher Steelers fans fell in love with is still absolutely there. His burst and bend remain unbelievable. 

That said, Herbig still has room to grow when it comes to finishing plays, especially if the team continues to experiment with him as an off-ball linebacker. Causing chaos alone can make a good front seven player, but making more of those tackles can take Herbig’s game to the next level. 

The big question of this article has been if these contracts are aging well through six weeks. With Herbig, I’d say “yes” with some caveats. His current AAV currently ranks between Nik Bonitto ($26.5 million) and the Jonathan Greenards, Andrew Van Ginkels, George Karlaftises of the league ($24.5 to $23 million) – right in the sweet spot between the “star” and “very good player” tiers of the position. And of course, that ranking will only move more in the Steelers’ favor as the market inflates in the years Herbig is under contract. It’s also worth noting his guarantees are far from crippling.

Herbig fits in that area of the market well right now, and his “it” factor as a pass rusher gives him the potential to move closer into star territory. Of course, the Steelers will have to give him more opportunities to get there first.

Final verdict: Living up to the new money, but still some questions about role on team.

Darnell Washington

New deal total: 4 years, $42 million (9th among tight ends)

AAV: $10.5 million (15th)

Guaranteed money at signing: $11.25 million (28th)

RP: Washington got the smallest of the three contract extensions that we’re examining today, and he also plays the position traditionally considered the least valuable between them. And yet, if you asked which of these three players would most noticeably have their absence felt, I would choose Washington.

Tight ends have become en vogue. Look no further than the league’s plummeting rates of 11-personnel (three wide receiver sets) usage. As recently as 2022, there were only 13 teams using 11-personnel at a rate below 60%, according to Sūmer Sports. In 2026, 21 teams have dipped below that threshold. The Steelers aren’t quite there yet — they sit at 61.2 % thanks to Aaron Rodgers and Mike McCarthy’s affinity for that grouping — but they have been trending down in recent weeks as they’ve lost receivers to injury and have leaned more into their running game.

But the Steelers aren’t exactly missing out on the tight end fad either. They use two tight end sets (12-personnel) 28.1% of the time, eighth most in the NFL. Only one receiver, DK Metcalf (391), has more snaps than Pat Freiermuth (284) and Washington (272).

You might be asking why tight ends are suddenly all the rage. To put it simply, it’s about creating matchup advantages. Not every tight end possesses the same skill set, but an ideal tight end is able to create plays as a pass catcher, as well as help provide better blocking than your typical wide receiver could thanks to their bigger size. What modern offenses have started figuring out is that by trotting out two or more tight ends, they can put opposing offenses in a bind. If defenses stay with lighter personnel — like nickel and dime packages with more defensive backs on the field — the offense can use the extra size tight ends provide to try to out-physical the defense in the run game by having bigger players. If defenses instead go heavier, with more linebackers or extra defensive linemen on the field, the offense can hunt matchups in the passing game by picking on the linebackers in coverage, or tricking them with play action.

That brings us back to Washington and the Steelers. While Freiermuth is the more prolific pass catcher, Washington has proven he can create explosive plays when targeted, and he has quickly been regarded as one of the better blocking tight ends in the league.

PFF grades aren’t perfect, but to give you an idea of Washington’s effectiveness, he’s got their fifth-highest run-blocking grade among tight ends with at least 80 run-blocking snaps this season. Increase that threshold to 100 snaps, and he has the second-highest grade among 20 tight ends with that kind of workload.

While I personally feel like there is still room for the Steelers to do more with Washington as a blocker —especially getting him on the move pre-snap — they have started to find more creative ways to deploy him as a blocker.

But it’s not just limited to the traditional running game; the Steelers are also finding ways to utilize Washington as a designed blocker in their passing attack.

And even when he isn’t technically blocking on a play downfield, he’s a great chess piece to use to stress or obstruct defenders in coverage to open up other playmakers. I would like to see the Steelers utilize Washington more in rub concepts to set legal picks, or in tandem with more receiver routes to help open up space for players like Germie Bernard, DK Metcalf, and Roman Wilson when he returns.

And while Washington doesn’t put up huge numbers as a pass catcher — 15 receptions, 156 yards, and two touchdowns so far — it still feels like there is untapped potential the Steelers could get from him in this area.

I don’t want to pretend Washington is perfect, however. I actually think the game against the Buccaneers might have been his worst of the season, despite scoring the touchdown.

He helped contribute to an interception early in the game.

There were also a handful of plays where sloppy technique got him beat as a blocker. Here were the two worst instances:

There was also a play where he was tagged with an illegal shift penalty that wiped what would have been a 3rd-and-16 conversion from Jaylen Warren in the red zone during the fourth quarter.

So no, Washington isn’t a perfect player. None are. But when you look at his body of work, and what he means to this offense, I lean towards him more than earning his money. Factor in that he has such low guaranteed money, and it truly feels like the Steelers got a bargain for one of the NFL’s unicorns.

Final verdict: Living up to the new money.

Keeanu Benton

New deal total:4 years, $72 million (18th among defensive linemen)

AAV: $18 million (T-25th)

Guaranteed money at signing: $14 million (48th)

RB: I’ll be honest, I didn’t expect Keeanu Benton to re-sign with the Steelers. I always thought he would be a player who would go on to play his best football with another team. Instead, he’ll be playing out his prime in the black and gold. 

Despite oozing with potential from his college days, Benton has long been a player Steelers fans have been somewhat lukewarm on in terms of his long-term potential. However, some of his upside started to show in 2025 when Benton broke out with 5.5 sacks despite still largely playing nose tackle – that’s rare pass-rushing juice for the position. 

Benton isn’t the tooliest of rushers, but his patented club/rip move remains deadly. In his recent seasons, he’s been good for a handful of play-breaking block sheds per game, often playing with the definition of “violent hands.” 

He’s an athletic defender who’s more than capable of generating highlight-reel plays. 

And while Benton’s pressure rate has slightly dipped so far this season (4.3% compared to 5.7% in 2025), I’d argue 2026 is shaping up to be his most impactful year yet, with performances against the Colts and Buccaneers in recent weeks that popped off the screen even if the box score stats weren’t gaudy. 

Playing less nose tackle in Patrick Graham’s defense, Benton has looked more comfortable against the run, getting blown off the ball less than he used to and dropping a knee at times to anchor against double teams. He isn’t a standout bull rusher, but has continued to pick up tricks from Cam Heyward, with three batted passes in the last two weeks and a number of well-timed leaps against Tampa Bay that seemed to disrupt the play. 

And despite Derrick Harmon being out for Pittsburgh as of late, Benton has played a large role in the effort that kept Bucky Irving to 2.4 yards per carry and Jonathan Taylor to just 3.0 in the last two weeks. Once the ageless Heyward finally does retire, Benton’s growth has indicated the team’s defensive line play won’t suddenly become a weakness, which is exactly why Pittsburgh kept the latter around. 

It’s also worth noting that while Benton’s contract might’ve been the most surprising per fans in terms of cost, it’s an accurate picture of where he fits in an expensive NFL defensive line market. Benton may be tied in terms of AAV with Heyward (who has been an absurdly good deal for Pittsburgh contract-wise in recent years), but remains in the tier of names such as Devonte Wyatt ($18.3 million) and Ed Oliver ($17 million), just above the tier of Tershawn Wharton and Javon Kinlaw (around $15 million). Even more than Herbig, Benton’s contract is shockingly low in terms of guarantees, as well. 

Benton’s big game against Tampa Bay continued to build the case that the Steelers made the right move in betting on the 25-year-old to keep growing as a long-term defensive piece. Don’t get too caught up in sack numbers for a defensive tackle – Benton has been a fun watch in 2026. 

Final verdict: Living up to the new money.

Join in on Steelers R&R by sharing your takes on this week’s topics. Feel free to pitch future questions in the comment section or on Twitter/X: tag @_Ryland_B or @RyanParishMedia, or email us at steelersreadnreact@gmail.com.

item.title: Week 7 NFL Survivor strategy and picks
item.description: David Fucillo provides NFL Survivor pool tips in Week 7, offering up safe, value, and trap picks.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome back for Week 7! We have three remaining undefeated teams, with the 49ers sitting at 6-0 and the Chiefs and Vikings at 5-0. The 49ers face both teams, so maybe later this season we get some undefeated vs. undefeated matchups!

The NFL returns to action with the playoff starting to pick up steam. November is when people really start digging in, but we’re at the point where teams are facing must-win situations. The Texans had one of those last week, beating the Jaguars in London to improve to 2-4. The Browns made a bit of a statement in coming back to beat a Lamar Jackson-less Ravens squad. The Saints got a big road win over the Giants to help their NFC South chances.

This week, the Giants and Texans are facing off in what is important for both teams. The Giants will send out J.J. McCarthy for his first start after replacing Jameis Winston last week. The NFC East is a disaster and if the Giants can move things along with McCarthy, it’s very winnable. The Texans finally have some momentum after a messy start and the AFC South is pretty wide open as well behind the Jaguars.

I’m back with my Week 7 Survivor picks ahead of Patriots-Bears on Thursday Night Football. Survivor involves picking one team each week to win. If they win you advance, if they lose you’re out in most cases. I’m in one pool with four entries, but it’s also a double-elimination pool. I’ve lost two of my entries, with the Cowboys stinging last week. I’m down to two entries, each of which has one strike. We’re riding a fine line!

Below I’ve got a look at the safest choices, best value picks, and then trap picks. I’ll post my own picks at the end. I’ll update on Sunday once I lock in my three picks for the weekend.

I’ve included odds for the favorite in each game, courtesy of FanDuel.

Safest picks

Texans (-10.5) over Giants

The Texans defense should be able to put J.J. McCarthy in a blender. And given how C.J. Stroud has been playing, I just don’t see how the Giants can keep up.

Best value picks

Texans (-10.5) over Giants
Vikings (-6.5) over Colts

You could save the Texans for Week 18, but that’s a long way off. The Vikings aren’t huge favorites, but there isn’t much reason left to use them the rest of this season.

Trap pick

Jets (-4.5) over Dolphins
Cowboys (-4.5) over Eagles

These are two divisional games involving four mediocre to bad teams. Stay away from them.

My picks this week

I have two entries left and I’m leaning toward using the Texans with one pick and the Vikings with the other.
