item.title: How much is Quenton Nelson worth on the trade market?
item.description: Nelson remains one of the best guards, but his age, contract and position make his trade value difficult to determine.
item.content:encoded:
This is the third and final part of a three-article series looking at the hypothetical trade value of three of the Colts’ biggest stars. This one is about Quenton Nelson. You can click here to read the previous two articles on Jonathan Taylor and DeForest Buckner.

As with Taylor and Buckner, this is not an argument that Indianapolis should trade Nelson. The Colts probably should not be looking to move any of these players unless the season falls apart or another team comes calling with an offer that is too good to ignore. The point of the series is simply to determine what these players would realistically be worth if serious trade interest developed around the deadline.

Of the three players, Nelson might be the most difficult to evaluate. He is 30 years old, still one of the best offensive linemen in football and has arguably the strongest individual résumé of anyone currently on the Colts roster. However, he plays a position that has historically struggled to command significant draft capital in trades, and his contract expires after this season.

That combination makes determining his value a lot more complicated than simply looking at his performance.

Nelson is still one of the NFL’s best guards

There really is not much debate about Nelson’s ability. Since Indianapolis selected him sixth overall in 2018, he has been one of the league’s most consistent and dominant offensive linemen.

Nelson has made the Pro Bowl in all eight of his completed NFL seasons, becoming just the second offensive lineman in league history to accomplish that feat. He has also earned six All-Pro selections, including three consecutive First-Team honors to begin his career. He is already building a very convincing Hall of Fame résumé, and at 30 years old, there is still plenty of reason to believe he has several productive seasons ahead of him.

His recent performance only strengthens that argument.

Nelson remains a dominant run blocker, capable of moving defenders off the line of scrimmage and creating running lanes that simply would not exist with an average guard. He is also a reliable pass protector and has been one of the few constants on an Indianapolis offensive line that has experienced considerable turnover around him.

There is no reason to believe a team acquiring Nelson would be paying for a player whose best football is already behind him. He is still performing at an elite level, and that should make him an attractive addition for teams looking to improve their offensive line.

The trade comparisons are surprisingly underwhelming

This is where Nelson’s evaluation gets interesting.

The best comparison is Joe Thuney, whom the Kansas City Chiefs traded to the Chicago Bears in March 2025 for a 2026 fourth-round pick. Thuney was 32 years old at the time and coming off another outstanding season. He had earned First-Team All-Pro honors, helped Kansas City reach its third consecutive Super Bowl and established himself as one of the most dependable interior offensive linemen in football. He had even demonstrated the versatility to play left tackle when the Chiefs needed him there. Despite all of that, Kansas City received just a fourth-round selection. There were reasons for the relatively modest return. Thuney was entering the final year of his contract, carried a substantial salary and the Chiefs needed financial flexibility. Chicago was also acquiring a player who would likely require another expensive contract to remain with the organization beyond 2025. The Bears eventually signed Thuney to a two-year, $35 million extension, meaning they surrendered just a fourth-round pick to acquire one of the NFL’s best guards before committing to him financially.

Another comparison is Jonah Jackson, whom the Los Angeles Rams traded to Chicago for a sixth-round pick during that same offseason. Jackson was only 28 years old and had previously made the Pro Bowl, but his value had declined considerably following an injury-plagued season in Los Angeles. Nelson is obviously a much much better player than Jackson, and that sixth-round return should not be considered a particularly useful indication of his value. Thuney, on the other hand, presents a legitimate benchmark.

Nelson is two years younger than Thuney was when Kansas City traded him and has an equally impressive, if not better, individual résumé. He is also still playing at an exceptionally high level, which should make him more valuable to a team considering a long-term extension. However, Thuney’s return shows just how difficult it can be to extract premium draft capital for an expensive veteran guard, regardless of how talented he is.

The positional difference matters, too. Teams have historically been much more willing to surrender first- and second-round picks for offensive tackles, particularly those capable of protecting a quarterback’s blind side. Guards are certainly important, especially with the number of dominant interior defensive linemen around the league, but the trade market has rarely reflected the same level of urgency.

Nelson may be one of the best players at his position, but that does not automatically make him worth a first- or second-round pick.

His contract makes him a potential rental

Like Buckner, Nelson is entering the final months of his current contract.

He signed a four-year, $80 million extension in 2022, making him the highest-paid guard in NFL history at the time. That deal expires after the 2026 season, meaning any team acquiring him at the deadline would have contractual control for only the remainder of the year.

His current cap hit is $24.2 million, although that number is somewhat misleading when discussing a potential trade.

Nelson has a $16 million base salary this season, along with a $2 million roster bonus that Indianapolis has already paid. His $6.2 million prorated signing-bonus charge would also remain with the Colts, meaning an acquiring team would only be responsible for the remaining portion of his base salary.

At approximately the halfway point of the season, that would amount to around $8 million, depending on the exact timing of the trade.

That is a manageable number for some contenders, particularly those with sufficient cap flexibility or the ability to restructure other contracts. The bigger concern would be what happens after the season.

Nelson will be 31 next year and could reasonably expect another lucrative multiyear deal. Considering the continued growth of the offensive guard market, it would not be surprising if he sought a contract worth more than $25 million annually.

An acquiring team would therefore have to decide whether it wants to surrender valuable draft capital for a player it may only control for a few months, or commit significant money to a guard entering his 30s.

That is a difficult combination, especially when considering the fourth-round pick Kansas City accepted for Thuney under similar contractual circumstances.

How much longer can Nelson play at this level?

This is where I think Nelson has a stronger argument than either Buckner or Taylor. At 30 years old, he is certainly no longer a young player, but offensive guards can remain highly productive well into their 30s. Much of the position relies on strength, technique, leverage and experience, all of which can help compensate for the gradual athletic decline that comes with age.

Thuney is a good example. He was still one of the league’s best guards at 32 and earned another substantial contract from Chicago. Zack Martin also remained among the NFL’s premier interior linemen into his 30s before injuries eventually caught up with him.

Nelson has the physical profile to follow a similar path. At 6-foot-5 and approximately 330 pounds, he possesses exceptional natural strength and has spent years developing the technique and understanding necessary to consistently win against some of the best defensive linemen in football. His durability is another important factor. Nelson has started at least 15 games in seven of his eight completed NFL seasons, including all 17 games in 2024 and 2025. There have been injuries along the way, but nothing that suggests his body is approaching a point where a significant decline should be expected. I would be comfortable projecting another three or four quality seasons from Nelson, provided he remains healthy. That does not mean he will necessarily maintain his current All-Pro level throughout that period, but there is little reason to believe he cannot remain a very good starting guard into his mid-30s.

For a team interested in extending him, that potential longevity is important. Unlike Buckner, whose future beyond the next couple of seasons is somewhat uncertain, Nelson could realistically provide several more years of high-level play.

The difficulty is that those future seasons are not included in his current contract. Any team that wants to secure them would have to negotiate and pay for them separately.

Who could use Nelson?

The market for Nelson would be somewhat unusual. Almost every team in the league would benefit from adding him, but relatively few would be willing to surrender a meaningful draft pick while simultaneously committing to another expensive contract.

Minnesota is one of the more interesting possibilities. The Vikings have experienced offensive line issues and have already been linked to the possibility of pursuing a significant upgrade before the trade deadline. Nelson would immediately strengthen their interior protection and provide an established veteran presence for an offense that could benefit enormously from greater consistency up front.

Baltimore is another team worth considering. The Ravens have invested heavily in their offensive line, including their acquisition of center Cam Jurgens, but there has already been discussion about whether they should pursue Nelson following the Colts’ organizational changes. Adding an All-Pro guard would give Baltimore another powerful blocker capable of improving both its running game and interior pass protection.

The biggest obstacle would be the financial commitment, particularly for a franchise that has already allocated considerable resources to other areas of its roster.

The New York Giants also make some sense, although their situation is different. Under John Harbaugh, New York has reason to prioritize building a more physical offensive line, and Nelson would fit that approach extremely well. The Giants would have to evaluate whether surrendering draft capital for a 30-year-old guard is consistent with their longer-term plans, but his ability to provide several more quality seasons makes the idea worth considering. If JJ McCarthy turns the team around, they could win that garbage division.

Las Vegas is another potential destination, particularly if the Raiders are looking beyond 2026. The Raiders have invested in several positions along their offensive line, but left guard remains an area where Nelson could provide an enormous upgrade. The appeal would be less about acquiring a short-term rental for a playoff push and more about bringing in an established All-Pro who could anchor the interior for the next several seasons.

Those are only a few possibilities, but they illustrate the challenge in determining Nelson’s market. He is talented enough to improve almost any team, yet the combination of his contract, age and positional value makes finding a realistic trade partner considerably more difficult.

So, what is Quenton Nelson worth?

I think Nelson has the strongest argument of the three players in this series for retaining a high level of performance over the next several seasons. He is still one of the best guards in football, has been remarkably consistent throughout his career and is young enough to justify another substantial contract. Unlike Taylor, whose position comes with considerable workload concerns, or Buckner, who is already 32 and approaching the later stages of his career, Nelson has a fairly convincing case for another three or four productive seasons.

However, the Thuney trade is difficult to overlook. Kansas City received only a fourth-round pick for an elite guard who was still performing at an All-Pro level. Nelson is younger and arguably has more productive football ahead of him, but the two players share the same contractual concerns, and neither plays a position that typically commands an enormous return.

My valuation would be:

A 2027 third-round pick.

I think there is a reasonable argument for a second-round selection, particularly if multiple contenders become interested and one believes Nelson could be the missing piece on its offensive line. His age, durability and continued elite production certainly justify a higher return than Thuney received.

However, a second-round pick would be an excellent outcome rather than something Indianapolis should necessarily expect. A third-round selection feels like a more realistic compromise. It would represent a meaningful premium over the Thuney trade while acknowledging the risk of acquiring an expensive veteran with no contractual control beyond the season.

There is also the compensatory pick argument to consider. If Nelson leaves Indianapolis in free agency, the Colts could potentially receive a compensatory selection in 2028. However, that would depend on the contract he signs elsewhere and the team’s own free-agent activity. There is no guarantee Indianapolis would receive a third-round pick, making a guaranteed selection in 2027 more appealing.

Of the three players examined in this series, Nelson might be the one I would be most reluctant to trade. He remains an elite offensive lineman, has shown little indication of slowing down and could be an important part of the franchise’s next competitive window, even if Indianapolis decides to make significant changes elsewhere on the roster.

That is ultimately what makes his situation so interesting. A third-round pick might be a fair reflection of his current trade market, but it would be difficult to argue that the Colts could replace what Nelson provides with that selection.

If Indianapolis believes it can return to contention relatively quickly, keeping Nelson and extending him may prove considerably more valuable than whatever draft compensation another team is willing to offer.

item.title: Panthers vs Buccaneers: Matchups to watch
item.description: Four matchups that are likely to determine the outcome of the Panthers vs the Buccaneers.
item.content:encoded:
The Carolina Panthers are coming off a comfortable win over the Philadelphia Eagles and their backup quarterback. That makes them 2-0 against backup quarterbacks so far in this young season. Up next is the Tamp Bay Buccaneers and either another backup quarterback or their starter fresh off a dislocated throwing thumb.

The Bucs have had a season from hell so far. They carried the negative momentum they ended last season with into this season. They got a random Thursday night win over the Cowboys with Jalon Daniels leading the charge. Otherwise, it’s been bad. They’re 1-5 and desperate for a win, or really anything to go right for them. Meanwhile, the Panthers are riding high on a two game winning streak against teams that were at least supposed to be good in the Lions and Eagles. They’ll be trying to extend their division lead. Here are the key matchups that will determine if that will happen.

Panthers interior offensive line vs Vita Vea

Vea doesn’t have a sack yet this season, and he’s only been credited with four tackles, but that doesn’t mean he’s no longer a factor along the defensive line. He’s not quite the player he used to be, but he’s still dangerous. He’s 15th in ESPN’s pass rush win rate for defensive tackles despite being double teamed on 81% of his pass rushing snaps. Robert Hunt has struggled this year, Damien Lewis is playing through his elbow injury, and Luke Fortner is Luke Fortner. They’re going to have their hands full with Vea, and they need to keep him contained so he doesn’t kill Bryce Young.

Bryce Young vs Alex Anzalone

The Buccaneers gave Anzalone a decent amount of money to step in for the retired Lavonte David as both the team’s defensive leader and coverage presence in the middle of the field. He has not lived up to the second part of that. He’s currently ranked dead last by Pro Football Focus among 75 linebackers that qualify. He’s been a huge liability in coverage and seems to have lost multiple steps in his age 32 season. The Panthers have found success in the middle of the field, particularly on RPO throws to Tetairoa McMillan and Jalen Coker. Given Anzalone’s struggles this year, those short passes in the middle of the field can turn into big chunk plays if the Panthers can continue to execute them with the same success they’ve had so far this year.

Bobby Okereke and Devin Lloyd vs Bucky Irving

Irving has been just about the only skill position player to have any sort of success for the Bucs this season. He’s averaging 4.7 yards per carry this season and showed how explosive he could be with 165 yards against the Cowboys while looking like vintage LeSean McCoy. If he gets into space, he’s one of the more slippery backs in the league. It’ll be on the Panthers linebackers to clog up his running lanes and prevent him from breaking into space where he can slip tackles and rip off long runs.

Baker Mayfield vs his thumb

Todd Bowles announced that Baker Mayfield will return to practice this week with eyes on returning to game action against the Panthers this weekend. We’re right at the beginning of Mayfield’s projected recovery timeline, so making it back for this game would be very aggressive. But like I said at the top, the Bucs are desperate, and that might lead them to go back to Baker, even if it’s a risky play. If Mayfield does play, you’d have to assume there will be some degradation in how well he can grip the ball. That gives the Panthers defense some extra opportunities to hunt turnovers, whether it be airmailed passes or strip sacks.

item.title: Lions Week 7 preview: Breaking down Packers’ offensive, defensive schemes
item.description: Breaking down the offensive and defensive schemes of the Green Bay Packers the Detroit Lions’ Week 7 opponent.
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions (3-2) and Green Bay Packers (4-2) will square off in Detroit’s first NFC North battle of the 2026 season.

“They’re playing really good football right now,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said of the Packers. “Two of their best games have been these back-to-back games. Plus-six in the turnover ratio the last two weeks; it was seven takeaways on defense, man. It’s an opportunistic defense. They fly around the football. They disguise well and create issues. […] it’s been an outstanding test for us. Hell of an opponent, first division game of the season at home. We’re looking forward to it, but this is a real good team right now playing good football.”

Let’s take a closer look at the Packers’ coaching staff, the scheme they run, and scouting notes from their most recently viewed games.

Packers head coach: Matt LaFleur

NFL coaching seasons: 18th (Texans, Washington, Falcons, Rams, Titans, Packers)
Head coaching seasons: 8th (Packers 2019-present)
Offensive coordinator: 2nd (Rams 2017, Titans 2018)
Other coaching roles held: QB coach, Offensive assistant
Influences: Mike Shanahan, Kyle Shanahan, and Sean McVay
Coached under: Both Shanahans, McVay, Gary Kubiak, Dan Quinn, Mike Vrabel
Play caller: Yes

Dan Campbell on LaFleur:

“Matt’s (LaFleur) doing a hell of a job. They have. They’ve gotten better every week. […] what Matt’s done over there and they’ve done offensively, they’ve evolved in areas, but there are some things that they’re going to hang their hat on. They’re good at and they’re not going to change that. They’ll just wrinkle it, man, a bunch of eye candy to try to get you off of it. And it’s effective. It’s still effective. It’s been effective every year.”

Offensive coordinator: Adam Stenavich

NFL coaching seasons: 10th (49ers, Packers)
Offensive coordinator seasons: 5th (Packers 2022-present)
Previous coaching positions: Run game coordinator, OL coach, Assistant OL coach
Playing career: 5 seasons on NFL practice squads (Panthers, Packers, Cowboys, Texans)
Influences: Kyle Shanahan and Matt LaFleur
Coached under: Shanahan and LaFleur

Offensive scheme

Passing game: West Coast Shanahan offense
Running scheme: Wide zone/Shanahan system, introduced more gap/trap/wham concepts
Scouting notes:

  • Core concepts of LaFleur’s scheme: Early down play-action, pre-snap motion, bunch formations, spread the ball around, vertical attack, explosives, screens, chip blocks are used to slow the pass rush, adaptability
  • Primarily utilize 11-personnel: 60% of the time — 12-personnel: 25%; 13-personnel: 15%
  • Efficient passing attack — 269.3 passing yards per game (5th)
  • Have moved the ball well; struggled to score touchdowns early in the season, but have improved
  • Pass yards per play: 7.5 (12th); EPA per pass: 0.05 (13th)
  • Red zone touchdown efficiency: 50% (22nd); Jordan Love EPA in red zone: -0.24 (32nd)
  • Deep ball is the strength of this offense, but also situational, as it is more frequently used when they have the lead (15.5%), but is not as prevalent when trailing (6.67%) — per Anthony Balaj’s film study
  • 3rd most explosive passing plays in the NFL
  • The deep ball also leads to big penalties; gained 135 yards on penalties on deep passes through six games
  • Majority of all targets go to top three skill players: WR Matthew Golden, WR Christian Watson, TE Tucker Kraft
  • Target share: Golden 26%, Watson 22%, Kraft 17% — That’s two-thirds of the passes thrown by Love
  • Offensive line play has been an issue, both in the pass and run game
  • Pressures allowed: 97 (29th); pressure rate: 40.2% (25th); quick pressure rate 22.1% (22nd)
  • Time to pressure: 2.36 seconds (32nd)
  • Jordan Love EPA when pressured: -0.26 (17th), per Sumer Sports
  • Run game has been, by far, the worst rushing attack in the NFL
  • Rushing yards per game: 59.8 (32nd); per carry: 2.9 (32nd); Rush EPA: -0.29 (32nd); success rate: 30.4% (32nd, per NextGenStats, via NFLPro); DVOA stuffed runs: 25% (32nd)
  • OL stats: PFF blocking grade: 47.3 (32nd); DVOA (32); adjusted yards (32nd)
  • RB Josh Jacobs is eligible to return, and while the Packers are playing coy, the Lions say they expect him to play — but how ready will he be after not playing football for the last month and a half?

Dan Campbell on Packers offense:

“They’ve settled some things in in that old line. […] (QB Jordan) Love, man. He makes it go. He is the secret sauce. And (WR Christian) Watson and (WR Matthew) Golden, man, they’re dangerous threats down the field and he’s going to give them opportunities that shows up every week. (TE Tucker) Kraft has come off the injury nicely. He’s gotten better every week. He’s playing good football right now. So, this team’s playing at a high level.”

Defensive coordinator: Jonathan Gannon

NFL coaching seasons: 16th (Falcons, Titans, Vikings, Colts, Eagles, Cardinals, Packers)
Defensive coordinator seasons: 3rd (Eagles 2021-22, Packers 2026)
Head coaching seasons: 3 seasons (Cardinals 2022-25)
Previous roles: DB coach, assistant DB coach, defensive quality control; Scout (Rams 2009-11)
Influences: Mike Zimmer, Matt Eberflus, Vic Fangio
Coached under: Zimmer, Eberflus, Jerry Gray, Emmitt Thomas; Nick Sirianni, Frank Reich, Bobby Petrino
Staff ties to Detroit: Daniel Bullocks (Packers CB coach — drafted by Detroit in the second round of the 2006 NFL Draft)

Dan Campbell on Gannon:

“Gannon’s doing a hell of a job with that defense too. They’ve just steadily gotten better and better and they’re playing at a very high level right now.”

Defensive scheme

Base: 3-4 hybrid Base
Coverage: Fangio zone principles, two-high split-zone safeties
Scouting notes:

  • 3-4 Base (23% of defensive sets), 2-4 Subpackage (Nickel: 75%)
  • Fangio zone principles, two-high split-zone safeties (65%); Lots of 3-safety sets
  • Off-Zone coverage: 78%; Man: 18%
  • Two-high safeties (65%): Cover-2: 21%; Cover-4: 26%; Cover-6: 10%; Cover-2 Man: 1%
  • Single-high safety (35%): Cover-3: 24%; Cover-1 Man: 10%
  • Cover-0: 5%
  • Two-high shell designed to limit explosive plays; Passing explosives allowed: 1.8% (Best in NFL)
  • Safeties Xavier McKinney and Evan Williams have been tremendous
  • Third-safety/NB Jonathan Bullard has leveled up his game in the slot
  • Disguising/simulating and timing of blitzes (31.7%) to create pressure has been effective
  • Pressures: 100 through six games (2nd most); Overall pressure rate: 41.2% (4th)
  • Non-blitz pressure rate: 35.4 (17th)
  • Rotate four EDGE players pretty evenly to keep fresh
  • Rotate four defensive tackles through 3- and 2-down DL fronts
  • Run defense has taken a step back under Gannon
  • Run defense DVOA: 26th
  • Rushing yards allowed: 114.3 per game (18th); 4.0 per play (15th)
  • Offenses heavily attacking the edges of this defense: Outside zone plays on 63% of run calls (2nd most)
  • Two problem areas that got them into trouble early in the season…
  • 3rd down defense: allowing a 44% conversion rate (25th)
  • Red zone touchdowns allowed: 75% conversion rate (27th)

item.title: Dolphins news: Speeding up team development, injury updates, Jets game prep
item.description: A collection of Miami Dolphins news from around the web, including Miami’s development system. injury updates, and looking toward the Jets in Week 7.
item.content:encoded:
The Miami Dolphins are the youngest team in the NFL this season, kick-starting their franchise rebuild with an influx of rookies and second-year players. The team hopes to move from a consistently mediocre franchise that fights just to make a cameo in the playoffs to one that consistently battles for deep postseason runs. While the goal is lofty, the Dolphins have had to tear down their roster for 2026, taking a massive immediate salary cap hit to get the future cap under control.

Development is the Dolphins’ name for the game, as they hope their young roster can learn and grow quickly. South Florida Sun Sentinel columnist Chris Perkins took a look at how Miami is hoping to speed along that learning curve with a weekly addition to the practice schedule:

Every Thursday, after the Miami Dolphins conclude their regular practice, many of the second- and third-team players gather for a brief 7-on-7 session. It sounds minimal, but coaches and players say the extra work is helpful because it better acquaints backups on Miami’s offense and defense, offers more hands-on coaching, and familiarizes them with playing alongside the starters…

“It’s been really important to me,” said [head coach Jeff] Hafley, who detests 7-on-7 sessions during training camp. “I think regardless of where you’re at, I think we’re still in a developmental league.”

The 7 on 7s are only seven or eight plays, but the repetitions and additional coaching add up over the course of a season for Dolphins backup players, most of whom spend midweek practices playing on the scout team.

And here’s the big thing: in the 7-on-7 sessions, backups run the Dolphins offense and defense, they’d run if they’re suddenly inserted into a game. When they play on the scout team during midweek practices, they run the opponent’s offense and defense.

item.description: Which team will it be? The Commanders next 8 opponents have combined record of 17-29-1; 6 have 4 or 5 losses in 6 games
item.content:encoded:
The Daily Slop – 22 October 2026

Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy!

Commanders links

Articles

Riggo’s Rag

Commanders’ bleak start hides a playoff opening that’s still within reach

Even with the second-worst record in the conference, the Commanders are only two games out of first place in their division. And if the team makes the necessary adjustments over their week off, that deficit could shrink quickly.

When the Commanders return to the field, they’ll play the Philadelphia Eagles at home without quarterback Jalen Hurts, who is done for the year with a scary blood clot situation.

After that, they’ll play the biggest disappointment in the NFL — with the only possible exception of the team they share a stadium with — the Los Angeles Rams.

If the Commanders win both of those games, they’re right back in business.

And it’ll only get better from there.

They’ll face the New York Giants on the road, who they should’ve beaten at home. They’ll host the ever-inconsistent Cincinnati Bengals. They’ll visit the Arizona Cardinals and Tennessee Titans, two teams they should beat regardless of the location. Then they’ll host the Houston Texans and Atlanta Falcons, both currently sub-.500 operations.

The Commanders should win at least five of those games. They can probably win all of them if they bring their best.

[U]n 2020, Washington started the season 2-7 and rallied to make the playoffs at 7-9.

This Commanders team is substantially more talented than that one was. That squad’s regular-season quarterbacks were Dwayne Haskins, Kyle Allen, and a one-legged Alex Smith. Its second-leading receiver was Cam Sims.

This team has Jayden Daniels under center. Even without McLaurin, Stefon Diggs, third-round rookie Antonio Williams, and Treylon Burks are still here. And first-year linebacker Sonny Styles is putting together a Defensive Rookie of the Year-caliber campaign just as Chase Young did then.

All the Commanders need to do is stay relatively healthy the rest of the way and let the rest of the NFC East keep imploding. Once they pick up one or two wins, which they’d better be able to do with this stretch coming up, they’ll have momentum and vibes on their side.

It looks bleak now. But that can change, and the bye week is the perfect time to refresh and map out the road ahead.

Sports Illustrated

With Terry McLaurin Out, Washington Must Change How It Uses Antonio Williams

[T]he reason they need to give him more looks is clear: he creates separation like no one else on the roster, and even though his snap share has stayed steady (hovering in the high 60s of late, even in London when McLaurin was out nursing a hamstring), he’s criminally underused in David Blough’s system.

Against San Francisco, Williams ran 35 routes but had only four targets, catching three for 50 yards. All four targets came on third down in the fourth quarter, and his three catches accounted for Washington’s only successful third-down conversions of the night. In an offense looking for answers, why ignore one?

A glance over Williams’ numbers above makes a major case for him to be involved earlier and more often, including plays where he’s the intended first read. PFF credits him with 69 run-blocking snaps and a 51.5 run-blocking grade, leaving room for improvement if Washington expands his role in two-receiver formations.

The bye gives Blough time to make Williams a bigger part of the plan from the opening drive. Give him designed opportunities on first and second down. Washington has a lot of production to replace with McLaurin out, and Williams has already shown he can handle more of that work.

Sports Illustrated

Commanders Quietly Added Former NFL Head Coach to Help Struggling Defense

Steve Wilks has joined Washington’s defensive staff to help Dan Quinn and Daronte Jones, but his role comes with an important limitation

According to NFL Insiders Mike Garafolo and Ian Rapoport, the Washington Commanders hired Steve Wilks to help the defensive staff ahead of the game against the 49ers. The decision to hire Wilks was made back in September, but he didn’t start working with the team until last week. Wilks will assist with game planning and will work under Quinn and defensive coordinator Daronte Jones; he will not be with the team on game days.

It’s important to stress that Wilks has no playcalling duties and is there to make the staff’s job easier. The real gauge will come after the bye, when everyone will see whether any consistency changes are visible, as adding another football mind doesn’t guarantee anything changes on the field.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

Athlon Sports

Commanders Expected to Make Some Tweaks During the Bye While Dan Quinn Keeps His Job

Dan Quinn bought himself time with the fight Washington showed in San Francisco, and the Commanders have already added Steve Wilks to help the defensive staff

The defense is where Wilks comes in. Jones’ unit has struggled to adjust after halftime, as we noted earlier this month, and Odafe Oweh’s slow start on a $100 million deal hasn’t helped. Sonny Styles, the NFL’s top defensive rookie at the quarter mark, gives Wilks a young piece to build around. Daron Payne, who has 12 sacks over the four seasons since his 2022 breakout, landed third on FOX Sports’ list of the best players who could be available before Nov. 10.

The offense took its own hit. Terry McLaurin tore his patellar tendon and will miss the rest of the season, Quinn said, per The Athletic’s Jonathan Jones, which leaves Daniels without his top target and the front office with trade options to explore.

Can the Commanders Fix Their Third-Down Problem Before Zack Baun and the Eagles Come to Town?

The Commanders get two weeks to fix third downs, the run game and Odafe Oweh’s pass rush before a 2-4 Eagles team brings Tanner McKee to Landover on Nov 1

Two weeks is a long time to sit on a 23-17 loss, and the Washington Commanders will spend their bye trying to fix the reason they keep losing close games. Monday night in Santa Clara, they converted 3 of 12 third downs against the 49ers. For the season they are 25 of 81, a 30.9% rate that ranks 31st in the NFL ahead of only Cleveland, according to NFL.com.

Washington went 0 of 4 on third down in the first half Monday, and the offense was flagged seven times for 66 yards. Holding calls on Josh Conerly Jr., Lucas Patrick and Brandon Coleman pushed drives backward, and Chris Paul’s face mask erased a go-ahead 31-yard touchdown run by Jeremy McNichols. We wrote that the offensive line keeps undoing what Jayden Daniels builds, and the third-down numbers back that up.

Baun is the reason the Eagles can survive without much else. He had 12 tackles, a tackle for loss and two pass breakups in the 24-22 opener at Lincoln Financial Field. Washington targeted him six times in coverage and gained minus-2 yards, and PFF gave him a 90.6 defensive grade, per the Eagles. He and Jalen Carter stuffed a third-and-1 in the first quarter, and Baun dropped a screen for a 7-yard loss in the second. Daniels needs manageable distances, and his line has to stop handing back 10 yards at a time.

Heavy.com

A third of the way through the season, Commanders offensive line continues to struggle

On Wednesday, PFF ranked the Commanders offensive line 20th in the league through six weeks.

“Washington’s front five combined to allow 18 pressures, eight of which were either sacks or quarterback hits,” wrote PFF’s Gordon McGuinness. “Right tackle Josh Conerly Jr. permitted six pressures on 51 pass-blocking snaps, a mark that led the team.”

Commanders writer Chad Ryan posted a chart on X that showed Daniels has had, on average, just 1.5 seconds before the pocket has collapsed on him this season. That’s the shortest amount of time in the league.

Entering Week 6, the Commanders were third in offensive line combinations according to Next Gen Stats.

But Quinn was very clear Tuesday. He won’t stop shuffling the offensive line until the unit plays a lot better.

Commanders.com

‘A real brother’: Tunsil provides invaluable mentorship to Commanders O-Line

Laremy Tunsil has not been on the field since he tore his triceps in training camp, but that does not mean he is absent from the Washington Commanders’ facility.

Actually, the five-time Pro Bowler is around quite a bit, and it has been a benefit for the team’s young offensive linemen.

“I think it’s been a blessing,” Josh Conerly said. “And it means a lot to us, as a group and for me personally.”

Tunsil might not be able to help the Commanders protect Jayden Daniels on game days, but the veteran is still finding ways to contribute while receiving treatment for his injury. He has been offering advice to the rest of the offensive linemen in the room and providing guidance on how they can improve their skill set. To the Commanders, it is more evidence of Tunsil’s leadership and how it has elevated the roster.

Dan Quinn continues to have every move dissected in a difficult season

“I’m sick about the ending,” Quinn said.

He should be. A win under these circumstances — against an unbeaten, smack-you-into-next-week team against which he trailed 23-3 in the fourth quarter — would have righted not only Quinn’s own ship, but would have yanked the Commanders back into the division race, leapfrogging the 2-4 Cowboys and Eagles.

The NFL’s message back? Who cares?

“We went out and we competed hard, but competed only gets you so far in this league,” Daniels said. “We got to do whatever it takes to win the game, and we didn’t win.”

Pick that quote up and attribute it to any Commander from so many games over the past year-and-change. It gets them nowhere. Since the beginning of last season, according to TruMedia, only five teams have a worse point differential than Washington — Tennessee, the New York Jets, Las Vegas, Arizona and Miami.

If that seems like the dregs of the league, well, that’s the company the Commanders now keep. At some point, your new house just settles into becoming part of the neighborhood.

The bye week, though, can’t just be about the players. If Quinn is to survive — and that’s not just for a Nov. 1 home game against Philadelphia, but into 2027 — he’s going to have to do some serious self-examination. Right now, he is good — and honest — about identifying problems. He’s not so good at fixing them.

The fact that a 20-point deficit didn’t spiral into another embarrassment likely gives Quinn the tiniest bit of wiggle room. A schedule that opens up — the 2-4 Eagles without Jalen Hurts, the 2-4 Rams who are a mess, Arizona and Tennessee beyond — provides opportunity.

But it is fair to ask what this team is building toward if the same problems keep showing up every week. If Dallas cannot establish a clear identity, clean up its mistakes or get consistent performances from its coaching staff and leaders, then talk about the draft will become more prominent.

Cowboys ‘run it back’ attitude on offense is starting to stumble

More simply put, the Cowboys “run it back” approach to hyping up all 11 starters returning on offense as a huge positive is not working, and this is another thing we’ve seen before as fans. The NFC East went winless. Again. Breaking down this dysfunctional division

The “NFC Least” bit was funny last week. Now it’s just sort of sad. For the second straight week, the entire division failed to muster a win, despite every team playing. It’s the first time in NFL history that’s happened, and it speaks to what kind of year it’s been for a division that’s been ravaged by injuries and decorated in disappointment. At the moment, the 3-2-1 Giants are pacing this lackluster race, but they can’t even decide on a starting quarterback (or a running back). The Cowboys and Eagles follow at 2-4, with Philly trying to figure out what to do next at QB after placing Jalen Hurts on injured reserve, while Dallas is simply trying to find any momentum on either side of the ball. Finally, there’s the 1-4-1 Commanders, who have actually looked plucky since Jayden Daniels’ return, yet continue to make all the wrong kinds of headlines.

What person in this division is facing the most heat?

There is a strong case to say Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni is facing the most heat — both deserved and undeserved. He spent Monday afternoon repeating that he was not a medical expert when reporters asked him how the Eagles managed Hurts’ blood clots. Indeed, he is not the authority on the medical situation. But it was an organizational misstep not to make those with authority on the situation available (the team’s medical staff reports to general manager Howie Roseman), or to at the very least brief Sirianni with necessary information. Meanwhile, the on-field product on offense is miserable.

The Commanders coach was eight days out from a nearly unforgivable game-management situation against the Giants when he introduced the possibility that he didn’t know what down it was. Quinn’s answer for that fourth-down play Monday night in San Francisco — that he absolutely knew what down it was, and that someone asked him if the Commanders could kick a field goal — is being scrutinized in the aftermath. It’s not an indication he’s making something up. It’s an indication that his every action — every timeout, every fourth-down, every personnel deployment — is under the microscope. That’s what happens when you win only four times in your last 18 tries.

Will the team you cover be a buyer before the deadline? Should they be?

There’s just no way. The Commanders shouldn’t be. They won’t be. And that’s even if they win their next two games against the 2-4 Eagles and the 2-4 Rams. (Is everyone out there 2-4?) It’s not just that their big “buy” move in the 2024 season, cornerback Marshon Lattimore, flopped. It’s that they have seven picks in the 2027 draft, and they clearly need as many of those to hit to rebuild a roster that, three years into the reign of general manager Adam Peters, needs both high-end talent and quality depth. If the Commanders make this a win-now year, it’ll be because they methodically stack wins against a slightly easier schedule filled with opponents who are dealing with serious injuries and other issues. It won’t be because they make a splashy move for a veteran player, sacrificing precious draft capital in the process.

Inside an NFL headset

The hidden world of technology, chaos, and split-second conversations behind every play

[Bill-in-Bangkok: I read this entire (and very long) article. If you have any interest in the topic, you might well find this deep dive fascinating. I only provided the intro paragraphs in this excerpt because it was too hard to mine a single nugget out of this article]

The hidden world inside NFL headsets is as complex and strategic as it is chaotic: a textured audio landscape of intense competition, stress, dramatically shifting emotions, unwritten rules and even absurdity.

From moment to moment, anything can happen.

Batteries die, communications get fuzzy (especially at certain stadiums) and paranoia flows. One coach demands silence as he calls a play, racing the play clock while his quarterback waits anxiously. Another flips channels to share praise or strategy, or to curse at someone.

A desperate assistant sneaks to a urinal midgame, standing shoulder-to-shoulder with fans, headset still over his ears — his relief disrupted by the voice of his furious boss looking for him on the sideline. Headsets erupt with joy after a touchdown or sack. A play call fails, and it’s swearing or worse: awkward silence.

“In the moment, it can be like, ‘Holy s—, what the f— are we doing? How is this a billion-dollar industry?’” Detroit Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing said. “And then there are other moments where you’re like, ‘Wow, that was so impressive.’”

item.title: Steelers' Yahya Black says he weighs 370 in mic'd up talk with 340-pound Tristan Wirfs
item.description: Buccaneers offensive tackle Tristan Wirfs doesn't often come across people bigger than him, but he did on Sunday, when he played against Steelers defensive tackle Yahya Black.
item.content:encoded:
Buccaneers offensive tackle Tristan Wirfs doesn't often come across people bigger than him, but he did on Sunday, when he played against Steelers defensive tackle Yahya Black.

Wirfs was mic’d up for NFL Films, which revealed an on-field conversation with Black about their respective sizes. The discussion went like this:

Black: "What they got you weighing at?"

Wirfs: "340. What about you?"

Black: "370"

Wirfs: "I knew it. You look huge."

Black: "Thank you. I try."

Wirfs: "No, I mean, you look great. You look like an absolute unit."

Wirfs and Black both played at Iowa, though not together. Wirfs' third and final year at Iowa was 2019, when he was a first-team All-American and won the Big Ten's lineman of the year award. Black's first year at Iowa was 2020, and Wirfs told teammates in the Buccaneers' huddle on Sunday that he visited Iowa after his rookie season in the NFL and met a younger and much smaller Black.

"When I went back to train after my rookie year, he was a freshman. He was not that big," Wirfs said in the Bucs' huddle. "He's, like, doubled in size."

Later, Wirfs complimented Black on his apparel when he attended a recent Iowa game as a spectator, and wondered where men their size can get clothes that fit.

Wirfs: "Where did you get your overalls for the Iowa game?"

Black: "Bro, I just walked into a shop downtown."

Wirfs: "No way!"

Black: "4X, baby."

Both Wirfs and Black have gained weight while in the league. Wirfs weighed in at 320 pounds at the 2020 Scouting Combine. Black weighed 336 at the 2025 Scouting Combine.

item.title: Hallmark's latest NFL movie is about the Bears. Where does it rank with Bills, Chiefs?
item.description: The Bears are the latest NFL team to get a "Holiday Touchdown" movie from Hallmark. Where does it rank?
item.content:encoded:
Hallmark has taken the field.

In recent years, the network has become an NFL fan, producing its famed holiday movies with a twist of action on the gridiron. An unlikely union on the surface, Hallmark and the NFL have proven to be a match on the big screen – or whatever screen you happen to watch it on.

Starting with the Kansas City Chiefs in 2024, Hallmark has released an NFL-themed love story in each of the last two years with the Buffalo Bills in 2025 and the Chicago Bears in 2026.

Filled with cameos from coaches, players, legends and more, each film has something that makes it unique. Hallmark movies are often known for cheesy storylines and nauseatingly happy endings, and the NFL series is no different.

But that is what people want for the holidays – even if that holiday is Christmas in July. The NFL is rarely a feel-good story for fans, unless your team is the one hoisting a Lombardi Trophy in February. In Hallmark though, everyone walks away feeling a little warmer than they did before pressing the "play" button.

And perhaps that's by design. If you're sitting there on a dark, chilly night wondering which Hallmark NFL movie to watch, this is for you – cozy blanket and hot drink not included.

NFL Hallmark movies ranked

3. Holiday Touchdown: A Chiefs Love Story (2024)

There's no need to sugarcoat it. Hallmark's NFL debut came up short and there was no need for a virtual measurement. It felt forced and lacked the synergy you'd like to see from the cast. No one will ever mistake Hallmark movies for the bigger-budget films produced by some of the world's biggest directors.

That's not the point.

"Holiday Touchdown: A Chiefs Love Story" felt like a movie that latched onto stereotypes of what it's like to be an NFL fan, rather than anything organic.

Most of the storyline centers on a lucky vintage beanie Santa gives one of the characters after they donate to a Salvation Army-style bucket. It's said that if you wear the hat on Christmas at the Chiefs game, then Kansas City's team is Super Bowl bound. Of course, the hat only guarantees the team will get there, not win it. After all, the magic has its limits.

That superstition is met with some skepticism by a new Chiefs employee, Derrick, who happens to be the team's director of fan engagement.

Of course, that skepticism is a slap in the face to Alana's family, who are in the running for the Chiefs' "Fan of the Year" award. The family operates a Chiefs fan store and isn't aware that Derrick is part of the group that will determine who gets the "Fan of the Year" honor.

Because this is Hallmark, Alana falls in love with Derrick and her family eventually wins the award after beating out a Chiefs' holiday display and a cat named "Catrick Mahomes."

Donna Kelce has the most prominent cameo appearance. Mecole Hardman, Trey Smith and Andy Reid are also featured in smaller speaking roles.

Like most things, the first attempt proved to be a learning experience for Hallmark – which needed a better storyline beyond "sports fans are superstitious."

2. Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story (2026)

The most recent entry in Hallmark's NFL catalog, the Bears took center stage in 2026, and it's clear how far the network has come since bursting onto the scene in 2024.

There was a real storyline associated with the Bears movie, combined with a cast that looked like it didn't just meet on filming days. Chicago's biggest win is that it doesn't force the NFL story like it had a mandate that came down from the league office. And that is where the movie shines, showing that football isn't always about the game. It's about the community it creates.

Matt's grandmother, Darlene, is about to attend her 500th Bears game. It's an occasion that wouldn't have been made possible if she hadn't attended a game at Soldier Field with her late husband many moons ago. The couple saw many highs and lows, including a Super Bowl. And it wouldn't be the Bears without references to the 1985 team.

Darlene ends up playing matchmaker for her firefighter grandson, who had been out of the dating game since his last girlfriend left for a better job in San Diego – a mutual decision.

Hallmark returns to its romantic roots in this movie, casting Avery as a freelance journalist who never opted to settle down in one place. Avery isn't a football fan, even though her mother and stepfather are die-hard Bears fans. Still, the journalist gets the opportunity to write about Darlene and the looming milestone.

Darlene, who is everywhere and nowhere at the same time, is constantly moving along to the next thing – allowing Avery and Matt to craft their own love story.

They eventually end up as a couple (did you really think they wouldn't), Avery opts to stay in Chicago and Darlene celebrates her 500th game, even if she almost missed it to take care of her neighbor that was recovering from cancer. She is eventually greeted by Mike Singletary and Charles "Peanut" Tillman at Soldier Field, shortly before a video from Caleb Williams plays on the jumbotron to commemorate the milestone.

Ben Johnson, Cole Kmet and Colston Loveland are among the cameos, but it wasn't really about the current team. The Bears movie opted instead to highlight the team's charity efforts, telling a story of resilience and overcoming life's obstacles.

This is your classic Hallmark movie, with a side of the NFL sprinkled in. The Bears aren't the story. They are just part of it.

If you want to escape reality for about 90 minutes without conflict, this movie is for you.

1. Holiday Touchdown: A Bills Love Story (2025)

Outside of the Green Bay Packers, there is no team in the NFL more perfect for a Hallmark movie than the Bills. It has the small-town feel. It has childhood friends who end up romantically involved, even if they were too afraid to admit their mutual interest.

In other words, it's everything you would expect from Hallmark.

The movie is almost like a blend of the other two on this list, even though it was the middle child of the NFL Hallmark series. The Bills are central to everything the movie does, but they aren't as overwhelming as the Chiefs or as distant as the Bears.

Consider it the "Goldilocks" of NFL involvement. Just right.

There is a clear buy-in from the Bills, with prominent cameos from Dion Dawkins and Damar Hamlin, Dawson Knox and others. Bills legends like Thurman Thomas, Andre Reed and Jim Kelly also joined the cast with now-former head coach Sean McDermott. And it wasn't just one scene for some of them. They made multiple appearances, making the story feel uniquely Buffalo.

The story follows Morgan and Gabe, two childhood friends who refuse to express their love for one another out of fear that it would ruin their existing relationship. The duo grew up next door to each other, with Morgan going on to be a doctor at the local hospital and Gabe becoming the president of stadium development for the new Highmark Stadium.

Together, the pair attempt to track down a mystery donor who helped support Morgan's family after her Uncle Tommy was drafted to fight in the Vietnam War. Now he receives a new Christmas ornament from the mysterious person every year.

Hoping to give him a Christmas to remember, Morgan and Gabe set out on a journey to identify the sender – who turns out to be Tommy's long-lost love interest, Mia. Eventually, Gabe orchestrates a surprise at the Bills game to reunite Tommy and Mia, proving that it's never too late for love.

By the end of the movie, Morgan and Gabe realize that they have feelings for each other and don't want to delay like her uncle did.

All of this is done with a clear love for the Bills, as families tailgate for the game on the front lawns of houses in the neighborhood – giving a Lambeau Field-like vibe. It has a splash of New York attitude and determination to it, evidenced by some pushy family members who aren't afraid to speak their minds.

The movie highlights the local children's hospital as part of the journey, along with the construction of the Bills' new stadium, which has since opened. With a central theme about expressing a love for community and legacy, the lasting message is a motivating one said by Tommy:

"In life, there’s gonna be pain," Tommy said. "And if you try to avoid it, it turns to regret. And you don’t want that living in your head rent-free. Time is a luxury. Don’t take it for granted.

"Take a chance."

If you're looking for a cozy Hallmark movie, perhaps Tommy's words are the best selling point.

item.title: Best Patriots trade targets to bolster team's Super Bowl 61 chances
item.description: The Patriots are hoping to make it to back-to-back Super Bowls, and improving their pass rush or WR room via trade could help them achieve that goal.
item.content:encoded:
The New England Patriots got off to a rocky, 1-2 start to the 2026 NFL season but have since turned it around.

The Patriots enter their Week 7 "Thursday Night Football" matchup against the Chicago Bears riding a three-game winning streak. They earned an impressive win over the Buffalo Bills before knocking off the Las Vegas Raiders and New York Jets to put themselves back in the early-season playoff race.

New England's path toward a second consecutive AFC title won't be easy, however. The Kansas City Chiefs are sitting at a formidable 5-0 entering Week 7 while the Bills, Denver Broncos, Jacksonville Jaguars and the entire AFC North could prove difficult outs come January.

With that in mind, Mike Vrabel and Eliot Wolf figure to explore potential upgrades for the Patriots ahead of the 2026 NFL trade deadline on Nov. 10. The Patriots have a talented roster overall, but there remain areas for the team to shore up at edge rusher, wide receiver and, potentially, running back.

Who are some of the top players the Patriots could target in potential trades? Here's a look at nine candidates for the team to consider, from big swings to modest additions.

Edge Maxx Crosby, Raiders

Will the Raiders trade Crosby in-season? Maybe not, but if they fall out of contention, they could consider moving him after their trade with the Baltimore Ravens fell through during the 2026 NFL offseason.

If Las Vegas does move on from Crosby, the Patriots should be very interested in his services. They are only three-deep on the edge currently and rank just 16th in pressure rate despite blitzing at the sixth-highest rate league-wide, per the NFL's Next Gen Stats.

Crosby, who plays with a relentless motor, would also be a nice cultural fit for Vrabel and Zak Kuhr's defense. The 29-year-old has posted 71.5 career sacks and 135 TFL in 116 career games and could be a nice, long-term partner for rookie Gabe Jacas.

Edge Josh Sweat, Cardinals

There will still be quality edge rushers on the market even if a big fish like Crosby isn't available. Sweat would be a nice consolation prize for the Patriots, as the nine-year veteran has a proven track record, averaging 8.5 sacks per game over the previous six seasons entering the 2026 campaign.

Sweat was also part of a Super Bowl-winning team with the Eagles in 2024. The Cardinals could be willing to part with the 29-year-old, and he would drastically improve both the team's depth and talent on the edge.

Edge Khalil Mack, Chargers

Mack is likely nearing the end of his illustrious career, but the 35-year-old is still producing at a solid clip. He has racked up three sacks and 18 pressures across six games despite playing for the lowly Chargers and could receive a jolt from joining a potential contender like the Patriots.

The impressive part of Mack's performance this season? He has still played 71.3% of the Chargers' defensive snaps. That Mack can still play a majority of the snaps will make him an even more attractive trade target for teams like the Patriots, as he can be used as either a starter or a rotational player.

WR Brian Thomas Jr., Jaguars

The Patriots improved their receiving corps drastically in the offseason by acquiring A.J. Brown, but they need to replenish their depth amid a slew of injuries. Mack Hollins and Romeo Doubs are on IR, so the team could stand to add more depth and talent behind Brown and DeMario Douglas.

Thomas could be an intriguing buy-low opportunity for the Patriots. The 2024 first-round pick has fallen out of favor in Jacksonville and played a season-low 15 offensive snaps against the Texans in Week 6. While the 24-year-old has struggled this season, he has averaged an impressive 14.5 yards per reception during his career and had 87 catches for 1,282 yards and 10 touchdowns as a rookie in 2024.

Perhaps Thomas simply needs a change of scenery to regain his form. With Drake Maye still on a rookie contract, the Patriots can afford to kick the tires on Thomas and see if he can develop into a quality No. 2 receiver across from Brown.

WR Quentin Johnston, Chargers

Johnson would be another upside swing for the Patriots. The 2023 first-round pick has a nice combination of size (6-2, 208 pounds) and speed but has been dogged by drops and general inconsistencies at the NFL level.

Even so, Johnston averaged 53 catches for 723 yards and eight touchdowns during the 2024 and 2025 NFL seasons. And while he hasn't found consistent success this season, he is averaging a dynamic 20.6 yards per reception, albeit on only eight catches. That, plus the fact that he is under team control through the 2027 season, could convince the Patriots to take a chance on molding him into a more consistent playmaker.

WR Jerry Jeudy, Browns

Browns coach Todd Monken spoke glowingly of Jeudy after the veteran helped Cleveland pull off a last-minute win against the Ravens in Week 6. Still, Jeudy is operating as the team's clear-cut No. 3 receiver, so the Browns may be willing to move on from him given that he's only in the second year of a three-year, $52.5 million contract.

Vrabel spent the 2024 season as a consultant with the Browns and has familiarity with Jeudy. The veteran coach may have a bigger role in mind for the 27-year-old and could target him to keep bolstering New England's depth at receiver.

WR Chris Godwin Jr., Buccaneers

Godwin may not have the same kind of tantalizing potential as Johnston or Thomas at this point in his career, but the 30-year-old veteran could be a reliable depth addition for the Patriots. He's a sure-handed pass-catcher and would work in tandem with Douglas to give New England different looks out of the slot.

Godwin is averaging a career-low 9.4 yards per reception this season, but he can still be a solid role player. It's just a matter of whether teams will be willing to take on his contract, which contains a $22 million base salary for the season.

RB Tyjae Spears, Titans

Should the Patriots be comfortable with the one-two punch they currently have at running back? Rhamondre Stevenson is averaging just 3.7 yards per carry this season while TreVeyon Henderson has dealt with injuries that have limited him to 4 yards per carry.

Stevenson remains a heady pass protector while Henderson's home-run speed could help him break out at any time. Still, the Patriots may want to add another option to the fold as they seek more consistent rushing success and provide insurance behind the oft-banged-up Henderson.

Options like Jonathan Taylor and Saquon Barkley could entice Patriots fans, but the team would more likely target a more modestly priced veteran to add to its rotation. Spears enjoyed his best season as a rookie in 2023, when Vrabel was coaching the Titans. A reunion in New England could help Spears tap back into his dual-threat capabilities as an explosive runner and a receiver.

Spears, 25, is on an expiring contract, so it wouldn't cost the Patriots much to land him in a trade.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Best Patriots trade targets to bolster team's Super Bowl 61 chances

item.title: Ravens QB Lamar Jackson returns to practice
item.description: Lamar Jackson was a limited participant in his first practice since suffering an ankle injury in week 4.
item.content:encoded:
The Baltimore Ravens are dealing with a laundry list of injuries entering Week 7, but Wednesday’s injury report included positive updates on several key players.

Chief among them was quarterback Lamar Jackson’s return to practice after a two-week absence due to an ankle injury. Head coach Jesse Minter twice used the word “preparation” when referring to Jackson’s participation, which was officially categorized as limited, and the two-time MVP was not in uniform when leaving the field. Taken together, those signs suggest that he is preparing to play but is not physically ready. Minter maintained his previous stance that the team was taking Jackson’s injury “day by day.”

Jackson’s preparation could have included taking snaps from Cam Jurgens as the two work to develop their chemistry and communication at the line of scrimmage. Wednesday was their first shared practice since the former Eagles center arrived in Baltimore via trade two weeks ago, as well as his first day of full participation with his new team. Jurgens spoke to reporters after practice, an excellent sign towards his availability for his Ravens debut on Sunday against the Bengals.

The Ravens listed 13 other players on their first injury report of Week 7. Here is the full list (* denotes new injury):

Full participation

  • TE Mark Andrews (full)
  • OLB Trey Hendrickson (finger)
  • C Cam Jurgens (concussion)

Limited participation

  • WR Rashod Bateman (shoulder)
  • S Jaylinn Hawkins (knee) *
  • TE Matthew Hibner (hand)
  • G/C Vega Ioane (ankle) *
  • LG John Simpson (groin)
  • LT Ronnie Stanley (non-injury related/rest, toe, ankle)
  • CB T.J. Tampa Jr. (knee, designated to return from injured reserve)
  • RG Andrew Vorhees (foot)
  • DT Broderick Washington (ankle)

Did not participate

  • DL Calais Campbell (non-injury related/rest)
  • OLB Tavius Robinson (pectoral)

Robinson’s injury is by far the most alarming. He leads the defense with 3.5 sacks and has been a crucial run-stopper off the edge. An absence would elevate undrafted rookie Ethan Burke into a larger role; he had two pressures in three pass-rushing snaps on Sunday in Cleveland.

The Bengals are coming into their trip to Baltimore much healthier after their bye week. Cincinnati reported just one injury on Wednesday: safety Kyle Dugger, who was limited with a quad injury. He appeared in the team’s first three games before going down with 41 snaps on defense and 49 on special teams.
